docs.title: rocm-bake
docs.text:
Reproducible builds of PyTorch, Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, vLLM and LMCache against ROCm, on a three-node BuildKit fleet, with every artifact published to a local OCI registry.

The build is one docker buildx bake file and one Makefile. Everything else exists to make that build fast, repeatable and measurable.

docs.title: What It Builds
docs.text:
PyTorch from source against ROCm, with Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, vLLM and LMCache on top, for gfx950 (default), gfx1201 and gfx1250.

Every pinned version is on the bake variables page, generated from rocm-bake.hcl — the single source for every value a build reads. make list-vars prints what is in effect; make version-check compares it against upstream and against the published wheels.

docs.title: Live Reports
docs.text:
Two lanes publish measurements continuously. They are not comparable with each other — see Live reports.

  • Fleet Runs ↗

    Every wheel across all three SNOC nodes at once, instrumented. Newest run, with a selector for every earlier one. The same chart serves a run still in flight — make perf-serve.

  • Nightly Builds ↗

    One warm bake per architecture on AWS CodeBuild, 02:17 UTC, published to ECR.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Commands run from the repository root on snoc-strix unless stated otherwise. make help lists every target; targets marked * build and push to the registry, which needs the ci login.

The repository is at sbates130272/rocm-bake and is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: From nothing to a published PyTorch image. On a fleet that is already set up, skip to step 5.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The fleet below is manifests/snoc.yml, which is what FLEET defaults to. Everything here reads that file, so a different fleet is a different manifest rather than a different set of instructions — see The fleet.

  • All nodes on the same Tailscale network.
  • snoc-strix: a gfx1151 GPU, Docker 27+. Runs the Zot registry, the shared compiler cache, and the GPU tests.
  • snoc-thinkstation, snoc-gaming: Docker 27+, reachable as ssh <host> from Strix. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4): they cross-compile for gfx950 fine but cannot run the test stage.
  • 200 GB+ of disk per node for the BuildKit cache.
docker --version
docker buildx version

The tailnet must bypass the corporate proxy

Every proxy-aware tool — curl, urllib, and the Go binaries including docker — tries to reach snoc-* through ZScaler and fails. The Makefile exports NO_PROXY_LIST for its own targets; anything run by hand needs the same in your shell profile:

export no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1,.ts.net,.local,10.0.0.0/8,100.64.0.0/10
export NO_PROXY="$no_proxy"

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:sbates130272/rocm-bake.git
cd rocm-bake

docs.title: Step 2 — Check Zot
docs.text:
Zot is the local OCI registry: published images, the BuildKit layer cache as OCI artifacts, and a pull-through mirror of Docker Hub, GHCR and Quay. It runs on Strix as a bare-metal systemd service, deployed outside this repository.

Do not start a second one

Other services pull through the same registry. Nothing here starts, stops or configures Zot — the zot-* targets only inspect it.

make zot-check      # is it active and answering?
make zot-catalog    # what does it hold?

Anonymous read is open; only pushing needs the ci account. Store that credential with pass, which is GPG-encrypted at rest and works over SSH — the secretservice helper fails with Cannot create an item in a locked collection unless gnome-keyring has been unlocked graphically.

sudo apt-get install -y pass golang-docker-credential-helpers
pass init <your-gpg-key-id>        # gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
# set "credsStore": "pass" in ~/.docker/config.json
docker login snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 -u ci
docker-credential-pass list        # verify it landed

One login on Strix covers the fleet: buildx sends registry auth to the builder as a session attachment.

Zot also needs a raised HTTP read timeout, or pushing the ROCm base fails — its largest layer is 8.67 GB and cannot cross a 1 Gb/s link inside Zot's 60-second default:

"http": {
  "readTimeout": "30m",
  "writeTimeout": "30m"
}

then sudo systemctl restart zot. Troubleshooting has what the failure looks like.

The registry serves plain HTTP over the tailnet, so the Docker daemon needs it in /etc/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "insecure-registries": ["snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"],
  "registry-mirrors": ["http://snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"]
}

make fleet-apply writes that file on every build node, from the manifest's registry.

docs.title: Step 3 — Create The Builders
docs.text:
make list-nodes             # which fleet this is, and what it declares
make builder-setup          # one builder per build node in the manifest
make builder-snoc-think     # or just one of them
make builder-status         # what exists now

There is no list of builders in the Makefile — builder-setup expands the manifest's node list. The remote nodes join over SSH to their Docker daemons, so neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates or the plugin.

Every builder gets a buildkitd.toml rendered for that node and --driver-opt network=host. Both are load-bearing:

  • the config carries plain HTTP to Zot, the pull-through mirrors and a [dns] block — BuildKit writes its own resolv.conf and defaults it to 8.8.8.8, so without the block a RUN step cannot resolve any tailnet name;
  • network=host gives the builder the host's resolver, MagicDNS included, which Docker strips from a bridged container's.

Both are fixed at create time

An existing builder does not pick up a later change. Adopting one costs that node's BuildKit content store: docker buildx rm snoc-strix && make builder-snoc-strix.

docs.title: Step 4 — Deploy The Shared Compiler Cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, all sharing one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules on Strix at :8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

sudo ./.builders/deploy-webdav.sh
make cache-check                 # can every node reach it?
make cache-summary               # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates

The port and path come from the manifest, so the deployer and the builders cannot disagree about where the store is. make fleet-check asks every node whether it can write to it, not just reach it: a node that can only read compiles everything and shares none of it, which looks exactly like a slow node.

Why a durable store, and why WebDAV

An in-RAM store loses the whole fleet's compiler cache on a power cycle; a plain directory tree survives and backs up with rsync. WebDAV rather than S3/MinIO because dl.min.io is blocked by the corporate proxy while nginx-extras is a normal apt install. Off the fleet, the nightly uses S3.

There is nothing to install on the other nodes.

docs.title: Step 5 — Build
docs.text:
make build-pytorch                    # one target on $(BUILDER)
make build-all                        # every target, one builder
make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # scheduled across all three nodes

BUILDER=snoc-pool is a sentinel, not a buildx builder: it routes through the balancer, one bake per target, results handed between nodes through Zot.

Each make build-* runs through telemetry/build.sh, which records duration, layer-cache hit ratio and sccache counters, then exits with the build's own status. TELEMETRY=0 skips it.

The build refuses to start when the compiler-cache store is unreachable, rather than silently recompiling everything:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

docs.title: Watch It
docs.text:
From a second terminal:

make build-watch                        # every builder, with a live tail
make build-watch WATCH_BUILDERS=snoc-think WATCH_LINES=40

Or one thing at a time:

make build-status     # records on $(BUILDER): running, completed, errored
make build-logs       # step output; BUILD=<id> for a specific record
make build-inspect    # duration, steps, cached steps, VCS revision
make builder-logs     # buildkitd's own log: registry, DNS, cache failures
make build-stop       # cancel builds started from this repo

build-logs is what the steps printed; builder-logs is the daemon underneath, where a registry, DNS or cache fault shows up while the build merely looks slow.

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify
docs.text:
make gpu-test GPU_HOST=snoc-thinkstation PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx1201

It checks per-dtype numerics on real hardware, and exists because a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd — an incorrect HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION once shipped undetected in every image.

By hand:

docker run --rm -it --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri \
  snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950

import torch
print(torch.__version__)           # 2.15.0+rocm10.1
print(torch.cuda.is_available())   # True
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

docs.title: Step 7 — Measure It
docs.text:
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold BUILDER=snoc-think
make bench-report

See Performance for what the four scenarios mean and how to read the numbers.

docs.title: Live Reports
docs.text:
Two lanes publish measurements continuously, to two pages on the gh-pages branch. Neither is committed to main — the data only exists where it was produced.

  • Fleet Runs — data/perf/

    Every wheel built across all three SNOC nodes at once, with CPU, memory, compiler-cache and registry traffic sampled throughout. Opens on the newest run, with a selector for every earlier one.

    Driven by hand with make perf-cold or make perf-warm, published with make perf-publish PUSH=1 from a build node. How it works.

  • Nightly Builds — data/nightly/

    One warm bake per architecture on a rented AWS CodeBuild machine, 02:17 UTC, published to ECR. Phase wall clock and cache-error counts, every run kept. A table, not a chart — see below.

    Fully automated, and it files a comment on one nightly-labelled issue as well. How it works, what it costs.

The two are not comparable

A fleet run is a parallel build across three nodes sharing a compiler cache. A nightly is sequential bakes on one rented machine, and its phase wall clock is the whole bake rather than a per-target cost. Quoting one as the other is the mistake both pages open by warning about.

A third set of numbers — isolated per-target costs under four cache conditions — lives on Performance, and is not comparable with either.

docs.title: Browsing Older Runs
docs.text:
Both pages keep everything ever published, and both open on the newest run — but they are not the same page, and only one of them charts.

data/perf/ is the interactive chart. perfsite.py writes a runs.json and a runs/<stamp>.json beside it, which the page fetches relative to its own URL to populate a selector; every run also keeps a data/perf/<stamp>/ permalink. Pick any past run from the dropdown and you get its full chart — overlaid CPU and memory, a legend that filters by builder and target, per-band hover.

data/nightly/ is a table, plus one bar chart. nightlysite.py writes a row per run and architecture — cold, warm, cost, sccache hit rate, layer-cache hits — with a data/nightly/<stamp>/ permalink and its own runs.json. Above the table, build-time.svg plots warm wall clock per night, one bar group per architecture. No legend filtering, no per-target spans, no sampled series.

The chart appears only once there are two runs to compare: one bar is not a series, and drawing it would imply a trend that cannot exist.

The sampled chart does not cover the AWS runs, and cannot

Not an oversight, and the distinction is narrower than "no chart". A rented CodeBuild machine has none of what the fleet chart is drawn from: there is no node_exporter on three nodes to sample into samples.jsonl, no per-target trace-<target>.json, and no Zot or nginx log to slice. None of that becomes available by wanting it.

What a nightly can see is its own wall clock, the instance it was billed on, and what its phase logs already printed — which is what build-time.svg and the cost and cache columns are drawn from, and nothing more. A nightly times bake invocations and claims nothing it cannot see.

nightlysite.py is deliberately a separate index for the same reason the admonition above gives. Merging the two selectors would put a parallel three-node run and a sequential one-machine run in the same dropdown, which is the not-comparable mistake made structural.

docs.title: Watching A Run Live
docs.text:
For fleet runs, the published page is not a different tool from the local one — perf-publish puts the chart perf-serve renders onto gh-pages and adds the cross-run selector. So the same interface works on a run that is still going:

make perf-serve             # newest run, http://<host>:8090
make perf-serve-status      # whether one is up, and where
make perf-serve-stop        # stop it, free PERF_PORT

It regenerates every 30 s and re-resolves which run is newest each cycle, so it picks up a run that starts after the server did. The page polls data.json rather than reloading, because the legend is the filter — a reload would discard whichever builders and targets you had narrowed to. A published run is frozen and stops polling.

perf-serve binds every interface

0.0.0.0 by default, because the usual viewer is a laptop on the LAN rather than on the tailnet. What that exposes is build telemetry — hostnames, CPU and memory figures, build step names — with no credentials and no registry access. Narrow it with PERF_BIND=<ip>, and make perf-serve-stop when you are done.

docs.title: Node Roles
docs.text:
snoc-strix is the default BUILDER and hosts both shared services. Its GPU is gfx1151; no node has a gfx950 card, which is the default build target, so make test only proves anything when PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH matches the hardware it runs on.

snoc-think and snoc-gaming are build capacity, joined to buildx over SSH to their Docker daemons, so neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates or the plugin. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4) and cross-compile for gfx950 without difficulty, but cannot run the test stage.

snoc-pool is a sentinel, not a node: it routes through .builders/balance.sh rather than to a buildx builder. See the balancer.

docs.title: Why A Tailnet
docs.text:
The three machines are not on one LAN, and the corporate proxy must never see tailnet traffic. Two consequences run through everything else:

  • no_proxy has to include .ts.net or every proxy-aware tool fails against snoc-*. The Makefile exports it; interactive shells need it in a profile.
  • Name resolution inside a build container is not the node's. BuildKit writes its own resolv.conf and defaults it to a public resolver, so .builders/buildkitd.toml.in carries a [dns] block listing MagicDNS first and two public resolvers after. The public entries are load-bearing: this tailnet has no global nameservers, so MagicDNS SERVFAILs on anything outside it and apt, pip and the PyTorch clone would all fail.

Even that was not enough for the compiler cache. Under load a tailnet lookup falls through to a public resolver, which answers NXDOMAIN, the search domain is appended, and the query becomes snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net.fold-leaffish.ts.net — 79 of 361 compiles lost in one Triton build. So the Makefile resolves the store's hostname once on the host, and build containers address it by IP.

docs.title: The Pieces
docs.text: Piece What It Is Owned Here? rocm-bake.hcl The build graph: 16 targets, 3 groups, 52 variables Yes Makefile A wrapper that reads every default out of rocm-bake.hcl Yes docker/Dockerfile.* Ten Dockerfiles; the build context is always the repo root Yes telemetry/build.sh Wraps a bake, emits Prometheus metrics, exits with bake's status Yes .builders/* Node setup, the balancer, the benchmark harness, registry readers Yes Zot OCI registry: images, layer cache, pull-through mirror No — zot.service nginx WebDAV sccache object store Deployed by .builders/deploy-webdav.sh node_exporter Scrapes the telemetry textfile on :9100 No

docs.title: Single Source Of Truth
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl owns every value a build reads. The Makefile keeps no copy: it parses the variable blocks at parse time and reads the defaults out. The two used to disagree silently — a make target and a bare docker buildx bake built different images from the same tree, and nothing said so.

.builders/check-defaults.py enforces it in CI, failing the build if a default is re-declared in the Makefile, if the Makefile reads a variable that does not exist, if $(call bake,…) names a missing target, or if WHEEL_REPOS drifts from the wheels group. The same pattern applies to serving/docker-compose.yml, which owns the runtime defaults.

docs.title: Build Graph
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl declares sixteen buildable targets. Bake derives the DAG from the contexts each names and orders it itself, so asking for vllm alone builds everything beneath it in dependency order.

    base["pytorch-base"]

    triton["triton-wheel<br/><i>noarch</i>"]
    cupy["cupy-wheel"]

    ptw["pytorch-wheel"]

    test["pytorch-test"]
    aiter["aiter-wheel"]

    nixl["nixl-wheel<br/><i>+ UCX from source</i>"]
    lmc["lmcache"]
    lmcw["lmcache-wheel"]

    rocm --> base
    src --> pt
    src --> ptw
    rocm --> run
    base --> triton

    triton --> pt
    pt --> ptw
    pt --> run

    nixl --> lmc
    cupy --> lmc

    nixl --> vllm
    lmcw --> vllm
    tv --> vllm

Five edges are not obvious from the names.

triton-wheel builds from the base, not from pytorch. Triton needs cmake<4 while PyTorch pulls cmake 4.x, so they cannot share an environment — which also lets Triton build in parallel with PyTorch. It is the only target with no architecture in its tag.

cupy-wheel hangs off the base too, because CuPy has no torch dependency. It is not optional: LMCache's MP server imports cupy at module scope, no published wheel fits this stack, and without it the server dies on the first request while vLLM waits five minutes before reporting a generic engine failure.

vllm consumes lmcache-wheel. vLLM ships the LMCache MP connector but imports lmcache.utils from it, so the wheel must exist first — and on the scheduled path, be published first.

lmcache takes no AITER context: its extension is cache movement, not GEMMs.

vllm consumes torchvision-wheel, which looks like an optional extra and is not. vLLM's build requirements pull timm, timm requires torchvision, and transformers' image_utils imports torchvision.io at module scope. PyPI publishes only CUDA builds of it, so without this edge the serving image carries a torchvision that cannot load on ROCm. It hangs off pytorch because its setup.py imports torch to decide it is building for ROCm at all — which is also why it cannot be installed into pytorch itself.

docs.title: How Inputs Are Wired
docs.text:
Targets take their inputs from siblings through target: named contexts — bake's dependency mechanism, and the only one it has.

contexts = USE_PUB ? {} : {
  triton-wheels = "target:triton-wheel"
  base-img      = "target:pytorch-base"
}
args = {
  TRITON_WHEEL_IMAGE = USE_PUB ? PUB_TRITON : "triton-wheels"
  BASE_IMAGE         = USE_PUB ? PUB_BASE   : "base-img"
}

A target with no context on its inputs is, as far as bake is concerned, independent — and may run concurrently with the thing it needs.

docs.title: PUBLISHED_INPUTS
docs.text:
Set PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 and every one of those contexts collapses to a registry reference; the PUB_* locals hold them and must track the tags of the target they mirror.

This is what makes cross-node scheduling possible: a target: context only works within one bake invocation, so one-bake-per-node would rebuild the whole chain rather than pulling what the previous stage pushed. pytorch-run is the exception — its context must resolve in both modes, so it uses docker-image://.

Note

PUBLISHED_INPUTS is read by bake from the environment, so it needs PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 make …, not make … PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1. Same for SCCACHE_LOG, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* overrides.

docs.title: The Balancer
docs.text:
buildx's multi-node builder does not balance: selection is by platform match, so when every node advertises linux/amd64 the choice ignores capacity — all five targets once landed on snoc-gaming (16 cores, 15 GB) while snoc-think (32 cores, 122 GB) sat idle. There is no hook to change it, so scheduling happens in .builders/balance.sh instead, one bake invocation per target pinned to a builder it picks.

make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # the usual way to build everything
make push-wheels BUILDER=snoc-pool    # just the wheel artifacts
.builders/balance.sh --dry-run        # what it would schedule, and where
.builders/balance.sh --best           # the strongest node right now

Nodes are scored by free GB of RAM plus idle cores, weighted equally on purpose: a cold PyTorch runs one cc1plus per core at 1–2 GB each, so RAM is what bounds a big node.

Work is scheduled from the dependency graph, not a list kept beside it. .builders/depgraph.py asks bake for each target's contexts, and balance.sh starts a target once every dependency inside the run has finished and been pushed, so what to build is a set (TARGETS="pytorch-wheel triton-wheel" .builders/balance.sh).

This replaced a hand-written STAGE_1..STAGE_5 — a second copy of what rocm-bake.hcl already stated, which drifted: a gfx1250 run scheduled vllm-wheel when no gfx1250 pytorch image existed, and died resolving it 0 s in, taking the rest of its node's queue with it.

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Before any build starts, every image the run resolves from the registry — minus the ones it publishes itself — is checked against Zot, so a missing input is named up front with the make target that creates it, rather than killing a target at step 1 after work is committed.

depgraph: these images are needed but not published, and nothing in
this run builds them:
  …/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx1250
      needed by: aiter-wheel, lmcache-wheel, nixl-wheel,
                 torchvision-wheel, vllm-wheel
   build it with: make push-pytorch

Only a 404 counts as absent: the corporate proxy answers 403 for the tailnet unless no_proxy covers it.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text: Among the targets eligible at any moment, the longest goes to the node that would finish it soonest, one build per node — several concurrent builds on one box each derive MAX_JOBS from MemAvailable as though alone, and oversubscribe it. The cost model is target-costs plus each node's link_mbps from the fleet manifest, ranked on finishing soonest rather than least loaded because this fleet's upload speeds span a factor of 25.

docs.title: Why build-all Refuses The Pool
docs.text:
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-pool errors rather than scheduling: every target would be its own bake invocation, so stage 2 would silently build against whatever is in the registry rather than what stage 1 produced. On a single builder the contexts resolve in-process and it is fine.

make push-all  BUILDER=snoc-pool    # scheduled, publishes
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-think   # single builder, no push

docs.title: MAX_JOBS
docs.text: Left empty, each build derives its job count from MemAvailable at 2 GB per job, sampled when the compile step starts — by which point its own earlier steps have taken memory. A cold PyTorch that settled at 21 GB derived 5 jobs where the same node gives a hot run 10, which is why the benchmark harness keys its results by job count.

docs.title: Telling Builds Apart
docs.text:
Every target stamps rocm-pytorch-build/<target>/<arch>/<RUN_ID> into its BuildKit history record. RUN_ID defaults to dev.

The prefix is this repository's name because a sibling project builds on the same nodes with the same convention and the same image names, and a shared prefix made its builds indistinguishable from these in make watch.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Four caches sit between a make build-pytorch and a from-scratch compile, and they are independent: a Dockerfile edit can drop layer reuse to 5% while sccache still serves every compile, and a changed compiler flag does the opposite.

flowchart LR
    build["a build step"]
    local["<b>1. BuildKit content store</b><br/>per node, local disk<br/>gckeepstorage 100GB"]
    layer["<b>2. Layer cache</b><br/>OCI artifacts in Zot<br/>two-tier: rolling + -ref"]
    sccache["<b>3. sccache</b><br/>nginx WebDAV on Strix :8081<br/>object files, fleet-wide"]
    pull["<b>4. Pull-through</b><br/>Zot mirrors Docker Hub,<br/>GHCR and Quay"]

    build --> local --> layer
    build --> sccache
    build --> pull

Each is removed by a different lever, which is what the benchmark scenarios are built on.

docs.title: 1. The Node's Content Store
docs.text: BuildKit keeps every blob it has pulled or produced on the node's disk, bounded by buildkit.gc_keep_storage in the fleet manifest. docker buildx prune is the only lever, and it is shared with any other project on that node.

docs.title: 2. The Layer Cache, In Zot
docs.text:
Each target exports its layers as OCI artifacts to a *-cache repository in Zot, so a layer built on one node is reusable from any of them.

Target Cache Repository rocm-runtime rocm-runtime-cache pytorch-base base-cache pytorch, pytorch-wheel pytorch-cache triton-wheel triton-wheel-cache aiter-wheel aiter-wheel-cache torchvision-wheel torchvision-wheel-cache pytorch-run runtime-cache cupy-wheel cupy-wheel-cache nixl-wheel nixl-wheel-cache vllm, vllm-wheel vllm-cache lmcache, lmcache-wheel lmcache-cache

docs.title: Two Tiers
docs.text: Reads always consult two refs: the rolling tag, and a frozen -ref baseline. Writes go to the rolling tag unless CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref (CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref make push-pytorch), which is how the baseline is deliberately refreshed. Without the second tier, one bad build overwrites the only cache everyone reads.

docs.title: Scoped By Architecture
docs.text:
Image tags have carried the architecture since ARCH_TAG landed; the cache refs did not. A gfx1201 build overwrote the gfx950 cache with layers gfx950 can never hit, and the next gfx950 build rebuilt cold and did the same back — so alternating architectures cost two cold builds, every time. CACHE_ARCH scopes those refs now.

triton-wheel stays on the shared ref deliberately: Triton is a compiler that publishes one noarch wheel. pytorch-base used to, and no longer does — it builds FROM rocm-runtime, whose kernel libraries are for one card, so one arch reading another's cache would take the wrong ones as a hit.

The unqualified base tag is no longer written

base:${ROCM_VERSION}-${PYTHON_VERSION} was published once for the whole fleet and is now ...-${ARCH_TAG}. Anything pinning the old form keeps resolving to the last image written under it, which gets staler from here. See Build targets.

Arch-sensitive targets also read the old unscoped latest, kept transitionally; it goes once each architecture has been built once.

Cache exports fail silently

Every cache-to carries ignore-error=true. A registry that is down, full, or refusing the push does not fail the build — it just means the next build has nothing to read. make builder-logs is where that shows up; the build itself only looks slow next time.

make layer-summary    # per image, most recent build, with the node it ran on
make build-inspect    # one build: duration, steps, cached steps

docs.title: 3. The Compiler Cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, all sharing one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules at /var/cache/sccache-webdav on Strix, port 8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT     http://<resolved-ip>:8081
SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX   rocm-pytorch
SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS          /tmp/sccache.sock
CMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER   sccache
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
CMAKE_HIP_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
HIP_CLANG_LAUNCHER          /usr/local/bin/sccache

Off the fleet the same cache runs on S3 — SCCACHE_BUCKET outranks the WebDAV endpoint, and an empty bucket name is treated as unset. See Building on AWS.

Three constraints make this work, and each fails quietly if broken.

A shared server is impossible. sccache's client sends a path, and the server reads and hashes the file itself — so a server on the host cannot see a build container's sources. Only storage can be shared.

The server is addressed over a unix socket, not a TCP port. The builders run with network=host, so a fixed port would be shared fleet-wide: a Triton build's client once connected to a concurrent PyTorch build's server, which could not see the files it was asked to hash. There is deliberately no port variable.

The store is addressed by IP, not by name — see the tailnet DNS problem. The Makefile resolves the host once, so setting SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT yourself only affects a bare bake.

docs.title: Refusing To Build Uncached
docs.text:
docker/Dockerfile.pytorch probes the store at image build time and refuses to start a compile when it is unreachable, rather than spending an hour rebuilding everything:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

The build prints sccache --show-stats as its last action, which is where the telemetry wrapper reads the counters — they cannot be queried afterwards, since the server dies with the build container.

docs.title: Inspecting The Store
docs.text:
make cache-summary    # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates
make cache-check      # can every build node reach it?
make cache-logs       # the WebDAV access log

cache-summary prints a delta and a rate as well as totals, because "+412 objects" means something very different over eight seconds than over an hour. The hit rate comes from the telemetry textfile, not the store: WebDAV has no stats verb.

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX is a directory in the store, so an experiment can run against an isolated namespace and delete it afterwards — which is what the benchmark harness does for its frozen and cold runs.

docs.title: 4. Pull-Through
docs.text:
.builders/buildkitd.toml.in points docker.io, ghcr.io and quay.io at Zot, which syncs them on demand. The ROCm base image is 8.67 GB in a single layer, so this is the difference between a build that starts in seconds and one that starts after a WAN transfer — which is what the frozen scenario measures.

What each cache is worth has a measured answer rather than an estimated one: see Performance.

docs.title: The Fleet
docs.text:
A build here needs machines, a registry to hand results between them, a compiler cache they share, and a scheduler that knows which is fast. That used to be written into the tools that use it: the node names appeared as literals in eight files, adding a node meant editing all eight, and standing the same fleet up elsewhere was not expressible at all. One file describes it now.

# manifests/snoc.yml
name: snoc
domain: fold-leaffish.ts.net
default_builder: snoc-strix
gpu_node: snoc-think

registry: {node: snoc-strix, port: 8080, managed: false}
cache:    {node: snoc-strix, port: 8081, dir: /var/cache/sccache-webdav}

nodes:
  - name: snoc-think
    host: snoc-thinkstation
    connection: ssh
    arch: gfx1201
    capabilities: [build, gpu, metrics]
    link_mbps: 90

make list-nodes                  # which manifest is in effect, and what it says
FLEET=<profile> make list-nodes  # a second manifest, if there is one

docs.title: What A Node Declares
docs.text:
host the address to reach it at. Not the same as name: the builder is snoc-think, the machine is snoc-thinkstation connection local or ssh. Exactly one node may be local arch the card it has — not the same claim as the gpu capability capabilities what it is for, below link_mbps upload throughput to the compiler-cache store colour its series colour in the perf report, optional

Capabilities are the vocabulary everything else speaks:

build takes bake targets gpu runs make gpu-test and the serving stack registry hosts Zot cache hosts the WebDAV compiler-cache store metrics runs node_exporter on :9100, sampled during a perf run

arch versus the gpu capability is the distinction that makes a cloud builder possible at all. Compiling for gfx950 does not need a gfx950 card — the fleet has none and cross-compiles for it daily; a card is needed only to run the result. A manifest that declares no GPU node says so and stops:

fleet <name> declares no gpu node, so there is nowhere to run this.
Either set GPU_HOST=<host> for a one-off, or give a node the 'gpu'
capability and name it in gpu_node:.

That message is the point. Before, GPU_HOST was a hostname with a default, and a fleet without one produced ssh ''.

docs.title: Who Reads It
docs.text:
.builders/fleet.py is the only YAML reader in the repository. Everything else takes the shape it can consume:

manifests/<fleet>.yml
        │
        └── fleet.py ──┬── --make        → Makefile (node list, registry,
                       │                   cache, GPU host, no_proxy)
                       ├── --nodes       → balance.sh's NODES
                       ├── --netmb       → balance.sh's link-cost term
                       ├── --endpoint    → bench.sh, builder-create.sh
                       ├── --buildkitd   → each builder's buildkitd.toml
                       ├── --inventory   → ansible/inventory/fleet.py
                       └── load()        → perfsample.py, perfreport.py,
                                           builder-health.py

The Makefile reads it in one pass at parse time, the same way it reads rocm-bake.hcl, and the builder targets follow from the node list rather than being written out — so a fourth node needs no Makefile edit:

FLEET_VARS := $(shell python3 -I .builders/fleet.py --make)
BUILDER    ?= $(call fleet_var,FLEET_DEFAULT_BUILDER)

builder-setup: $(addprefix builder-,$(FLEET_NODES))
builder-%:
    @.builders/builder-create.sh $*

docs.title: Where The Boundary With rocm-bake.hcl Is
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl says what is built; the manifest says where. Versions, refs, build args and the target graph are bake's. The registry, the compiler-cache store and which machines exist are the manifest's — because a second fleet is a second set of those, and a FLEET=... make push-all publishing to the SNOC registry would be the worst available failure: silent, and onto someone else's machine.

rocm-bake.hcl keeps its own REGISTRY and SCCACHE_WEBDAV_* defaults for a bare docker buildx bake driven without make, and check-contracts.py fails the build if those stop agreeing with the default manifest.

docs.title: The Scheduler Reads It Too
docs.text:
balance.sh charges a target's cache export against the node's link, because the fleet's uplinks differ by a factor of 25 — 3000 MB/s on the store host, 90 wired, 3.7 over WiFi. Scheduling on build time alone once sent triton-wheel's 6 GB export to the WiFi node, where the upload took ~28 minutes against the ~4 it took to build.

Those figures live in the manifest as link_mbps: because they describe the fleet; build and cache costs stay in target-costs because they are the same wherever the target runs. On a fleet whose nodes share one uplink speed the term cancels and placement collapses to plain LPT.

docs.title: Ansible
docs.text:
The manifest describes the fleet; Ansible makes a machine match it. Same file, same reader — ansible/inventory/fleet.py is a dynamic inventory over it, and the groups are the capabilities, so a play says what a node is for rather than naming machines.

make fleet-apply                      # converge every node
make fleet-apply ANSIBLE_FLAGS=--check
make fleet-check                      # read-only acceptance test
Role Hosts What It Owns common all base packages, no_proxy, tailnet status docker builders daemon config for the fleet registry, version floor registry registry_nodes Zot — installed when registry.managed, verified otherwise sccache_store cache_nodes the nginx WebDAV store node_exporter metrics_nodes the exporter and its textfile collector gpu gpu_nodes /dev/kfd, the render gid buildkit localhost the buildx builders, created from here

Two deliberate restraints. The registry role refuses to start a Zot the manifest says it does not manage — other services pull through it and it is deployed outside this repository. And the sccache_store role copies deploy-webdav.sh to the node and runs it rather than templating the nginx config, because check-contracts.py asserts that script's log_format still parses with the regex perfreport.py reads it back with. A Jinja copy would be a second thing to keep in step, and the one that drifted would be the one nothing checks.

make fleet-check asks each node whether it can reach the registry, read the cache, write to the cache, and export metrics. The write is the one that matters: a node that can only read compiles everything it is given and shares none of it, which looks exactly like a slow node.

docs.title: Adding A Node
docs.text:
1. Add it to manifests/<fleet>.yml with its capabilities and a measured link_mbps.
  2. make list-nodes — it should appear.
  3. make fleet-apply --limit <node>.
  4. make builder-<node>.
  5. .builders/balance.sh --dry-run — it should be in the plan.

Nothing else needs editing. That is the whole claim.

docs.title: Multiple GFX Targets
docs.text:
Two different things, easy to confuse:

What It Produces PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH='gfx950;gfx1201' One fat build, both code objects in one binary, one set of tags ARCHES='gfx950 gfx1201' Two builds, two separately-tagged sets of artifacts

PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH picks the architecture for one build and defaults to gfx950. ARCHES is the list the arches-* wrappers fan out over, and defaults to gfx950 gfx1201 gfx1151 gfx1250.

make arches-push-all                      # every target, every arch
make arches-push-wheels                   # just the wheel artifacts
make arches-build-pytorch ARCHES=gfx1201  # narrow it while iterating
make arches-list                          # what ARCHES resolves to

arches-% accepts any target name. Each architecture is a full pass over every target, so treat the list as a multiplier on build time; the passes run sequentially because they contend for the same builders.

docs.title: gfx1151 Is The Card snoc-strix Actually Has
docs.text:
RDNA3.5 (Strix Halo). Unlike gfx950 and gfx1250, it is in the fleet — see manifests/*.yml or make list-nodes for which node has what — so it can be GPU-tested rather than only cross-compiled, including with GPU_HOST=snoc-strix when the default gpu_node is busy.

ROCm 10.1 ships eleven -gfx1151 packages, so rocm-prune has something to keep. AITER v0.1.28 lists it as Experimental and still recommends installing it on RDNA parts, with the caveat that drives the PREBUILD_KERNELS choice below: most CK and ASM kernels are CDNA-only, so level 2 fails here as it does on gfx1201. Level 0 is the default.

It is not RDNA4 despite being gfx11-and-up — IS_RDNA4 tests for a gfx12 substring, so USE_ROCM_CK_SDPA_GFX12 stays off.

docs.title: gfx1250 Is In The List Without Being In The Fleet
docs.text:
The builders cross-compile — no node has a gfx950 card, yet the fleet builds it daily — so having no card only means make gpu-test cannot cover it. The ROCm 10.1 toolchain compiles it:

clang -x hip --offload-arch=gfx1250 -nogpulib -c   # exits 0

docs.title: gfx1250 Is Not RDNA, Despite The Number
docs.text:
This is the one place the architecture naming actively misleads, and the build branches on it:

ARCH_RDNA_TEST = replace(PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH, "gfx125", "")
IS_RDNA4       = ARCH_RDNA_TEST != replace(ARCH_RDNA_TEST, "gfx12", "")

gfx1250 and gfx1251 are gfx12-numbered but MI450-class datacenter parts: upstream LLVM gates amdgpu-sched-strategy=coexec on gfx1250 and gfx950 together, and gives gfx1250 tensor instructions no RDNA part has. A bare gfx12 test applies RDNA-only settings to a datacenter card, which is why the strip comes first.

AITER's kernel prebuild is level 0 on every architecture: build time is the binding constraint here, and the prebuild buys first-inference latency rather than capability, since AITER JIT-compiles on first use either way.

A measurement forced that before cost chose it. On gfx1201 all 13 844 kernels compiled and the build failed in the JIT module phase — 6 of 68 modules carry CDNA-only code and setup.py treats a failure as fatal, so bdist_wheel exited 1 after 51 minutes with no wheel. Reproduced twice; upstream lists gfx1201 as Experimental.

PREBUILD_KERNELS pins a level for one build. Level 2 produces no wheel at all on gfx1201 and gfx125x, so a global pin is only safe on CDNA.

docs.title: The Layer Cache Is Scoped By Architecture
docs.text: CACHE_ARCH keeps each architecture's registry cache separate, because before it existed alternating architectures cost two cold builds every time. triton-wheel stays on the shared ref — it compiles no device code — and pytorch-base does not. See Caching.

docs.title: Per-Architecture Pip Index
docs.text:
Every wheel here has an architecture-independent filename. torch is torch-…-cp314-cp314-linux_x86_64.whl whether it was built for gfx950 or gfx1201, and amd_aiter is 131 MB for one architecture and 481 MB for the other. In one directory they overwrite each other and --find-links serves whichever landed last. So the architecture lives in the path.

make wheel-index                  # fetch per arch, generate the indexes
make wheel-index-check            # install each one into a throwaway venv
python3 -m http.server 8081 --directory dist

pip install \
  --index-url http://<host>:8081/index/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]"

rocm-torch is a metapackage generated per index by .builders/wheelindex.py; its device-<arch> extra pins every wheel in that index at once, and each index declares only its own architecture's extra, so asking gfx950's index for [device-gfx1201] fails rather than installing mismatched binaries.

Wheels are fetched by architecture-specific tag, never :latest — written by whichever architecture was pushed last, with the wheels inside indistinguishable afterwards, which is the failure this index exists to prevent.

--extra-index-url is not optional

--index-url replaces PyPI outright, and the first ordinary dependency — numpy, via triton-kernels — then fails to resolve. download.pytorch.org has the same property and the same workaround.

docs.title: Publishing The Index Publicly
docs.text:
make wheels-publish ARCH=gfx950 puts one architecture on the public internet. It is a separate decision from building, so it is in no group and no push-all; run make wheel-index first and this publishes what that fetched, rather than fetching again.

The binaries and the index go to different places, and the split is forced rather than chosen. A wheel here is 300–500 MB — amd_aiter for gfx950 is 495 MB — and GitHub refuses any file over 100 MB in git. So gh-pages carries the index, which is 28 KB of HTML, and the wheels go to a release, where an asset may be 2 GB and does not count against the repository.

wheelindex.py --wheel-url already existed for exactly this: it sets the href prefix, and every link already carries a #sha256= fragment, so an offsite asset is still verified by pip at install time.

One release per architecture. Assets within a release share a namespace, and these wheel filenames are architecture-independent — two architectures' torch wheels are the same string and differ by 50 MB. In one release the second upload would collide with the first. That is the same problem the per-architecture index path exists to solve, so it gets the same answer.

make wheel-index                       # fetch and build the indexes
make wheels-publish-dry ARCH=gfx950    # show what would happen
make wheels-publish ARCH=gfx950        # release + gh-pages

pip install \
  --index-url https://sbates130272.github.io/rocm-bake/data/wheels/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]"

A downloaded asset does not say what it needs

The filenames carry no ROCm version and no architecture — torch-2.15.0a0+git31a77fc-cp314-cp314-linux_x86_64.whl is the same string for every target. Installing through the index is always correct, because the index path and the rocm-torch metapackage both carry the architecture. Downloading a release asset by hand is not: nothing in the file says it needs ROCm 10.1 and gfx950. torchvision and atom already carry +rocm10.1.0; torch, triton and amd_aiter do not yet.

docs.title: Why device-<arch> And Not A Variant
docs.text:
This is the shape TheRock ships ROCm in, rather than the WheelNext variant mechanism. Variants (PEP 817/825) are the better long-term answer, but both PEPs are Draft, installer support is prototype-only forks of pip and uv, and AMD's published provider matches PyTorch 2.9 on ROCm 6.3/6.4 against a gfx list without gfx950.

The extra is spelled device-<arch> so that when variants do land the architecture is already a first-class coordinate.

CI builds two architectures' indexes on every pull request and asserts that each installs its own and only its own.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Two builds of the same commit must produce the same image digest — because the digest is what every downstream FROM pins, and one that moves invalidates the entire chain below it. Three mechanisms get there, each added after the absence of it cost a full rebuild.

docs.title: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
docs.text:
BUILD_DATE only reaches the created label. The image config has a created field of its own, stamped with nanosecond wall-clock time regardless — so two builds of identical content produced different digests and every downstream FROM missed. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pins it.

It is set per image, not per repository, and it is a constant:

variable "SDE_EPOCH" { default = "1700000000" }

Two earlier designs failed. Taking it from HEAD gave the base a new digest on every commit, hence a full downstream rebuild even for a commit that touched only the Makefile — measured, Dockerfile.base unchanged yet the base digest moved 91db3c2e → aa52684f. Taking it from the Dockerfile's own last commit used history as a proxy for "this image's inputs changed", and the proxy does not hold: squashing 26 commits into 3 made every remaining commit touch every Dockerfile, so all five values collapsed and every cache was invalidated at once.

Content should decide, and already does — it decides the layer digests. The config created field carries no information anyone reads; the real build date lives in org.opencontainers.image.created. Pinning it to a constant costs nothing and survives history being rewritten.

Bump SDE_EPOCH only to force every image to a new digest deliberately. Per-image overrides pin one without the others:

SDE_PYTORCH=1700000001 make build-pytorch

The twelve SDE_* per-image variables all default to empty, meaning "use SDE_EPOCH". Bake reads them from the environment, so SDE_PYTORCH=… make … works and make … SDE_PYTORCH=… does not.

docs.title: atom-wheel Is Not Bit-Reproducible, And SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH Cannot Fix It
docs.text:
ATOM's atom/mesh/build.rs stamps the binary with chrono::Utc::now(), which no epoch variable reaches:

set_env!("BUILD_TIME", chrono::Utc::now().format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S UTC"));

Measured by comparing the gfx950 and gfx1151 wheels of ATOM v0.1.9, built an hour apart. Of 1206 files, 1204 are byte-identical; only atom/mesh/target/release/libmesh.so and the RECORD that carries its hash differ. Inside that 20,930,632-byte .so, exactly 24 bytes differ — 20 of them the .note.gnu.build-id, which is a hash of the output rather than an input, and the other four the digits of:

2026-11-05 02:13:25 UTC     gfx950
2026-11-05 03:12:52 UTC     gfx1151

Everything else in that record matches: crate version 0.2.0, target triple, ATOM commit 606aceb1, clean tree, rustc 1.95.0.

Two things follow. First, the wheel's content really is architecture-independent — which is what docker/Dockerfile.atom and the atom-wheel target claim, and the 1204 identical files are the evidence. Second, two builds of the same ATOM tag will never share a digest, so nothing downstream can pin atom-wheel by digest and expect a rebuild to match. Fixing it means patching build.rs to honour SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, upstream or in this repo; until then this is a known exception rather than a defect to hunt.

docs.title: Provenance Attestations
docs.text:
Provenance attestations record build timestamps, so they differ on every build even when the image is byte-identical — and because the attestation shares an OCI index with the image manifest, that changes the digest a downstream FROM pins. Measured: two identical base builds produced indexes fd260117 and 9c5e5112 around one unchanged manifest 91db3c2e, and a probe RUN missed across them.

So provenance is disabled on every image that is a parent or a named context — pytorch-base, pytorch, triton-wheel, and pytorch-wheel by inheritance:

NO_PROVENANCE = ["type=provenance,disabled=true"]

pytorch-run, aiter-wheel, torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm and lmcache keep theirs — nothing inherits a layer stack from them, so their digests may churn freely.

That is a weaker claim than "nothing builds FROM them", and the weaker one is the true one: Dockerfile.vllm does say FROM ${AITER_WHEEL_IMAGE} and the same for nixl, lmcache and torchvision. Those stages exist only to be bind-mounted from, and each is a scratch image holding one wheel — so a churned digest re-runs the pip install that was going to run anyway, rather than invalidating a chain of expensive layers underneath it. The cost that made NO_PROVENANCE worth having on pytorch-base is not present here.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
Labels live in the image config, so a changing revision or created gives an image a new digest even when its content is identical — the same trap, by a different route. Everything that ships gets full OCI provenance; pytorch-base gets identity only:

OCI_LABELS = {
  "org.opencontainers.image.source"   = SOURCE_URL
  "org.opencontainers.image.revision" = VCS_REF
  "org.opencontainers.image.created"  = BUILD_DATE
}
BASE_LABELS = {
  "org.opencontainers.image.source" = SOURCE_URL
}

Without that, a changing revision would give the base a new digest on every commit, re-cloning PyTorch's submodule tree each time. The base is an intermediate and should stay content-addressed.

docs.title: VCS_REF And Dirty Trees
docs.text:
VCS_REF is the short commit hash, with -dirty appended when the tree has uncommitted changes, so an image built from edited sources cannot be mistaken for the commit it came from. It also drives an immutable tag on every target:

…/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950-g<sha>

BUILD_DATE is the commit's own timestamp, not "now", for the same reason SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is pinned.

docs.title: Checking It Still Holds
docs.text: The warm benchmark scenario exists as a standing check on this: a new commit should cost nothing, so warm should build exactly what hot builds. The result is the assertion rather than the number — if warm diverges from hot, some per-commit value has found its way back into an image digest. That has happened twice.

docs.title: Serving Stack
docs.text:
vLLM, LMCache and NIXL, built from source against this repository's torch rather than installed from published wheels.

They have to be: their native extensions link against torch's C++ ABI, so a wheel built for AMD's ROCm 7.x torch and one built here cannot share a process.

docs.title: What Gets Built
docs.text:
Target What It Is nixl-wheel NIXL plus UCX, compiled from source with --with-rocm cupy-wheel CuPy for ROCm; LMCache's MP server imports it at module scope torchvision-wheel torchvision for ROCm; timm pulls it in and transformers imports it at module scope vllm / vllm-wheel The serving image and its wheel lmcache / lmcache-wheel The multi-process cache runtime and its wheel 
make push-serving              # nixl + cupy + torchvision + vllm + lmcache
make build-vllm                # just vLLM, single builder, no push
make fetch-nixl-wheel          # pull a wheel artifact into ./dist
make push-serving VLLM_REF=v0.31.0 NIXL_REF=v1.5.0

Every ref here is a release tag, never a branch: a moving ref would be served from the layer cache indefinitely once built, so an "update" would silently be a no-op.

Ubuntu's libucx is compiled without ROCm memory-type support, so NIXL bundles its own: Dockerfile.nixl compiles UCX with --with-rocm and auditwheel bundles it. Without that, every device-memory transfer bounces through host staging.

docs.title: Running It
docs.text:
serving/docker-compose.yml runs vLLM and the LMCache MP server as a pair over DOCKER_HOST=ssh://$GPU_HOST, so the file stays under version control here while the engine runs on the machine with the GPU.

make serve-stack               # vLLM + LMCache MP
make serve-vllm                # vLLM alone — the no-offload baseline
make serve-wait                # block until /health answers
make serve-test                # prove the cache is actually working
make serve-test-l2             # prove the disk tier serves blocks
make serve-logs                # both containers, merged, live
make serve-status              # what is running on GPU_HOST
make serve-down                # stop and remove

The compose file owns the runtime defaults the way rocm-bake.hcl owns the build ones, and the Makefile reads ${NAME:-default} out of it.

Variable Default What It Does KV_TIER cpu cpu = L1 only, file = L1 plus an L2 on disk TRANSFER_MODE lmcache_driven auto, engine_driven or lmcache_driven HSA_IPC_LEGACY 1 Required for cross-container HIP IPC VLLM_DEV_MODE 0 1 exposes /reset_prefix_cache, which serve-test needs L1_SIZE_GB 8 LMCache's host-RAM tier CHUNK_SIZE 256 Tokens per cached chunk MAX_MODEL_LEN 8192 GPU_UTIL 0.90 SERVE_MODEL Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct VLLM_BIND 0.0.0.0 from the Makefile, 127.0.0.1 in compose

A variable is passed only when actually set — an exported empty variable is still set, so VAR= would override the compose default with "".

VLLM_BIND differs deliberately: 127.0.0.1 is right locally, but driving it from another machine needs the port off loopback. Narrow it again, or tunnel, if the host is not on a trusted network.

HSA_ENABLE_IPC_MODE_LEGACY decides whether this works at all

It governs whether the two containers can share KV memory. When it is wrong the stack fails at startup, and no amount of TRANSFER_MODE tuning will fix it.

docs.title: The Tags Come From The GPU Host
docs.text: SERVE_ARCH asks GPU_HOST which GPU it has, via rocminfo over SSH. The build default is gfx950 while the serving host here is a gfx1201 RX 9070 XT, so deriving the serving tag from the build architecture asked Zot for an image nobody had built — the only symptom being a pull failure naming a plausible-looking tag. It falls back to the build architecture when the host is unreachable.

docs.title: /health Is Not Evidence
docs.text:
LMCache on ROCm has a failure mode where the endpoint serves every request correctly and caches nothing — in LMCache#4419 a reporter ran eight days at a zero hit rate with no error anywhere.

make serve-test sends the same long prefix twice, requires the second prefill to be measurably cheaper, then reads LMCache's own log for the store and the retrieve — vLLM's own prefix caching can make the timing alone look fine. serve-test-l2 goes further, emptying LMCache's L1 as well as vLLM's VRAM between requests so a hit can only have come off disk; it needs KV_TIER=file.

make serve-logs merges both streams tagged by container rather than using compose logs. The useful lines alternate — vLLM says what it asked for, LMCache whether it had it — and reading them apart once hid LMCache dying on a missing CuPy while vLLM waited five minutes before reporting a generic engine error.

docs.title: Running The Images Directly
docs.text:
# vLLM. AITER is installed but off by default.
docker run --rm --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri -p 8000:8000 \
    -e VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/vllm:latest \
    serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B

# LMCache's MP deployment: a controller holding the cluster-wide index,
# and one or more cache servers holding the blocks. The image has no
# default role — name the CLI you want.
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/lmcache:latest \
    lmcache_controller --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9000

docker run --rm --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri -p 8100:8100 \
    snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/lmcache:latest \
    lmcache_server 0.0.0.0 8100 cpu

The two LMCache CLIs take arguments differently

lmcache_controller takes flags. lmcache_server takes three positional arguments — host, port, storage. Giving the server flags makes it print a usage line and exit 1.

docs.title: Three Upstream Constraints
docs.text:
LMCache declares requires-python >=3.10,<3.14. This lane is cp314, because Ubuntu 26.04 — the only base AMD publishes ROCm 10.1 for — ships no other Python. The wheel is installed with --ignore-requires-python; the extension is compiled here against this interpreter, so the ABI matches by construction.

Both projects' requirement files carry CUDA-only or x86-wheel-only pins — cufile-python, nvtx, tilelang, amd-quark and others. These are stripped before the build, which also keeps them out of the wheel's install_requires. The lists are the VLLM_DROP_REQS and LMCACHE_DROP_REQS build args, so a dependency can be let back in once it has a usable wheel.

Upstream publishes torchvision only as a CUDA wheel, so this pipeline builds it, the way it builds torch and triton. It used to take PyPI's: timm pulls torchvision in through vLLM's build requirements, its _C_stable.so links libtorch_cuda and libc10_cuda, and import torchvision failed at load time. Nothing in the text-model path touches it, so the build and the import checks stayed green while vision and video models would have failed at serve time — and serving papered over it by swapping in the CPU wheel at container start.

torchvision-wheel replaces all of that. Dockerfile.torchvision builds it FROM the PyTorch image with FORCE_CUDA=1 (a BuildKit RUN has no /dev/kfd, so torch.cuda.is_available() is false and without it the wheel ships no device code at all) and asserts the result carries code objects for the target architecture before publishing. /etc/pip-constraints.txt now pins torchvision alongside torch and triton, to a +rocm<version> local version PyPI cannot offer, so any later resolution that reaches for the CUDA build fails loudly. The proof it worked is in Dockerfile.vllm: the LMCache connector import check, which could not run while torchvision was broken, is back.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Day-to-day running of the fleet.

docs.title: Routine
docs.text:
make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool    # build and publish everything, scheduled
make build-watch                   # follow it from a second terminal
make layer-summary                 # how much of each image was rebuilt
make cache-summary                 # is the compiler cache taking objects?

push-all with the pool sentinel is the usual way to build. Everything else is diagnosis.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
make fleet-check      # the whole fleet, against what the manifest claims
make zot-check        # registry active and answering
make cache-check      # every node can reach the compiler cache
make builder-health   # which builders can take work
make builder-status   # all builders and their nodes
make builder-load     # CPU, cores and load per node
make version-check    # are any upstream pins behind?

fleet-check is the one to run first: it asks every node in the manifest whether it can reach the registry, read and write the compiler cache, and export metrics. The targets under it ask one of those questions each.

make fleet-apply is the other half — it makes a node match the manifest rather than reporting that it does not. Run it when the fleet is idle: it can restart dockerd, stopping every container on the node including a builder mid-build. builder-health is what builder-ensure gates every build target on, so a build against a dead node fails fast rather than hanging.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text:
Five workflows. Every pull-request check runs on a GitHub-hosted runner and builds no real image — the images need a build fleet — so the PR gate validates structure and agreement rather than output.

The exception is the nightly, which does build: a warm run per architecture on AWS CodeBuild, published to ECR, reported as a GitHub issue and to data/nightly/. SNOC runs no CI job at all — it is driven by hand. See CI runners and Building on AWS.

CI — Dockerfile & bake validation runs on pull requests and pushes to main, path-filtered to the build files. It enumerates the bake targets into a matrix and checks, per target, that bake --print resolves, that the Dockerfile exists, and that the cache ref and the tags agree about the architecture. It also builds two architectures' pip indexes and asserts each installs its own and only its own, runs check-defaults.py, validates the serving compose file, HCL-lints the bake file, renders a synthetic perf report, and runs check-contracts.py over the producer/parser pairs.

Lint & spelling runs codespell, shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint, yamllint and ruff, plus make version-scrub-check. That last gate lives here rather than in ci.yml because ci.yml is path-filtered to the build files — README.md and docs/ are not in that list, so a pull request that hand-edited the version table would have run no job at all.

Build & push — ROCm PyTorch is workflow_dispatch only.

Version check — upstream releases runs Mondays and opens or comments on a single tracking issue when a pin is behind upstream. It uses the same .builders/versioncheck.py an operator runs, with the published-wheels column skipped: the registry is a tailnet name a GitHub runner cannot resolve, and an empty column would read as "we have published nothing".

Docs builds this site and deploys it to gh-pages, preserving the data/ directory already on that branch — that is where the published results live.

docs.title: Cleaning Up
docs.text:
make clean         # built images, locally, for every arch in ARCHES
make clean-cache   # cache images, locally
docker system df   # what is using the disk
docker system prune -a

Both clean targets are local only. The registry has to be pruned separately, and clean-cache covers only four of the ten cache repositories.

docker buildx prune is fleet-shared

These builders are shared with another project. Pruning a node's BuildKit store empties its layers too. The frozen benchmark scenario does this deliberately, which is why it is not in the nightly rotation.

docs.title: When Something Is Wrong
docs.text: Troubleshooting covers the failures that have actually happened on this fleet, with the log line that identifies each one.

docs.title: Building On AWS
docs.text:
AWS runs one thing for this repository: the nightly. A CodeBuild machine builds every target for one architecture, pushes the images to ECR, and shares a compiler cache on S3 with nothing else. There is no rented fleet, and no instance to stop.

CI runners covers the CodeBuild project itself — the runs-on label, the webhook, the security boundary. This page is the rest of the account, and what a night costs.

.builders/codebuild-setup.sh        # creates all of it, idempotently

docs.title: What The Account Holds
docs.text:
CodeBuild project One runner project, EC2 compute, privileged ECR 23 repositories — images plus their *-cache siblings S3 rocm-bake-sccache-<account>, 30-day object expiry IAM One service role, scoped to those two and nothing else

The *-cache repositories carry a 14-image lifecycle policy. They hold BuildKit's mode=max exports, which is every intermediate layer rather than the ones in the final image, and without a policy they grow without bound.

The compiler cache is S3 because sccache speaks it natively and a rented machine has no WebDAV endpoint to reach. SCCACHE_BUCKET outranks SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT in the Dockerfiles, and an empty bucket name is treated as unset — so the same bake file serves both fleets, and the SNOC nodes keep nginx.

docs.title: What A Night Costs
docs.text:
Measured, on the first full run: $13.94.

duration 1h09m, 13 targets, gfx1201 billed 69.7 min × $0.20/min cache errors 0 Scenario Cost Basis warm, one arch ~$14 measured warm, three arches ~$42 3× measured; arches are independent cold + warm, one arch ~$28 unmeasured; cold roughly doubles it

The schedule is warm-only, which puts a quiet month at about $420 at one architecture. A cold run pushes nothing and deletes its own sccache prefix, so it buys a measurement and nothing else — ask for it deliberately with -f run_cold=true.

ECR and S3 round to nothing against that. Build minutes are the bill.

Credential lifetime is the thing to watch

CodeBuild vends temporary credentials, and nightly.sh snapshots them with no refresh. A session lapsing mid-build turns every cache operation into a 403 — silently, because ignore-error=true hides it and the preflight has already passed. It held across 67 minutes. If a cold run ever pushes past about two hours, watch the cache-error column.

docs.title: Why Not A Rented Fleet
docs.text:
The obvious alternative is to rebuild the SNOC fleet on EC2 — three large builders and a services node, scheduled by balance.sh. It was specified and not built, for a measurable reason.

balance.sh resolves the targets into nine waves. Using the per-target figures in target-costs, the total work is 9089 s and the sum of the wave maxima is 8835 s — a parallelism headroom of roughly 1.03×. The chain runs pytorch-base → triton-wheel → pytorch-wheel → pytorch → … → vllm-wheel → vllm, with two 2336 s targets in the middle of it. A second builder buys almost nothing, and three idle instances cost the same whether they build or not.

Fanning targets out also costs. On one machine pytorch's inputs are already in the local BuildKit store when it starts; across machines that edge becomes a registry pull, and the cache rows in target-costs total ~17.6 GB per run.

So the matrix axis is architecture, not target. gfx950, gfx1201 and gfx1250 share no edges and no ordering, which is where splitting the work actually buys something — and a CodeBuild job per architecture gets it without owning an instance.

Two caveats on those numbers

They are measured on snoc-think (32 cores), not on CodeBuild — absolute times differ, the shape does not. And pytorch-wheel and pytorch are both recorded at 2336 s, as are vllm-wheel and vllm at 1409 s, which looks like one compile attributed to two target names. If so the true critical path is shorter than 8835 s and the graph is more serial, not less.

docs.title: Why Lambda Is Not The Builder
docs.text:
A fleet that only exists while CI runs is the obvious next thought, and the obvious implementation — a Lambda that runs the job — does not work. Every limit is breached by a wide margin:

Lambda limit A pytorch-wheel build 900 s per invocation vs hours 10,240 MB memory vs 4 GiB per core across 48+ cores 10,240 MB /tmp vs tens of GB of sources and objects no Docker daemon vs BuildKit needs one

The 15-minute ceiling cannot be raised by request. Lambda Managed Instances reach 90 minutes for asynchronous invocations, still an order of magnitude short, and the memory, storage and daemon problems remain. Persistent storage does not rescue it either: Lambda can mount EFS, but storage was never the binding constraint.

Two things that sound like escapes and are not: Lambda layers are not Docker layers (five maximum, 250 MB unzipped), and Lambda's container-image support means Lambda running an image, not building one.

CodeBuild's own Lambda compute mode inherits all of it — AWS documents it as supporting no Docker builds or runs, no privileged mode, no caching and nothing over 15 minutes. The nightly needs EC2 compute mode.

docs.title: CI Runners
docs.text: Pull-request checks run on GitHub-hosted runners — free, fork-safe, needing nothing from the fleet. The nightly builds: a Docker daemon, tens of GB of disk, hours of wall clock. This page is that machine; Building on AWS is its cost.

docs.title: SNOC Is Not It
docs.text: The fleet is driven by hand and registers no runner: it holds the registry, the compiler cache and the tailnet, and a runner there would be one docker group membership from root on all three.

docs.title: AWS CodeBuild
docs.text:
CodeBuild is a managed build service billed per build-minute; EC2 compute mode gives privileged mode (so BuildKit has a daemon), up to 72 vCPU and 824 GB of SSD, and timeouts in hours.

It can also act as a GitHub Actions runner: it takes the WORKFLOW_JOB_QUEUED webhook, registers an ephemeral runner for one job, then terminates it. Workflows name it:

runs-on:
  - codebuild-<project>-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
  - instance-size:2xlarge

The trailing segments override image and instance size per job: one project serves the matrix.

Offline runners are the steady state

A CodeBuild runner exists for one job and goes Offline the moment it ends. An empty or all-offline runner list is healthy here.

The alternative is philips-labs/terraform-aws-github-runner: a Lambda handler, launch template, builder AMI tracking ansible/roles/, GitHub App, orphan sweep. CodeBuild is one project and a webhook.

EC2 compute mode, not Lambda compute mode. Lambda allows no Docker builds, no privileged mode, no caching and nothing over 15 minutes; Building on AWS has the table, and the measurement saying a multi-node fleet would not have been faster anyway.

docs.title: Fork Pull Requests, And Why An if: Is Not The Boundary
docs.text:
A CodeBuild runner is self-hosted: it runs whatever the workflow says, under the project's IAM role. The obvious guard is a job condition:

# NOT sufficient on its own
if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository

Worth having, not a boundary. ci.yml triggers on pull_request, not pull_request_target, so the file that runs for a fork PR is the fork's copy, and .github/workflows/** is inside its own paths: filter — a fork edits the condition out in the same PR that exploits it.

The repository is public; the controls that hold are outside the workflow file:

  1. Require approval for all outside collaborators, not just first-time contributors — the default lets a repeat author run unapproved.
  2. Filter the CodeBuild webhook — an AWS-side control a fork cannot edit.
  3. Prefer scheduled and dispatch triggers. A schedule: run uses the default branch's workflow file, which no fork can rewrite — hence Dockerfile checks in the nightly, not the PR gate.

GitHub's guidance is blunter: no self-hosted runners on public repositories. Scope the IAM role as if a stranger's code will run on it.

docs.title: Standing The Project Up
docs.text:
.builders/codebuild-setup.sh does it idempotently and prints the gh variable set lines:

  1. A CodeBuild project — type Runner project, provider GitHub, location Repository — on EC2 compute, privileged mode on.
  2. A webhook on WORKFLOW_JOB_QUEUED — without it, no jobs.
  3. A service role scoped to the ECR repositories and the S3 cache bucket, nothing more. The build does not need write access to this repository — the report is published by a separate GitHub-hosted job.
  4. Repository variables, so the workflow needs no secrets:
gh variable set CODEBUILD_PROJECT --body <project-name>
gh variable set ECR_REGISTRY      --body <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com
gh variable set AWS_REGION        --body <region>
gh variable set NIGHTLY_ARCHES    --body gfx1201        # optional
gh variable set NIGHTLY_ENABLED   --body true           # last

NIGHTLY_ENABLED is the off switch and belongs last: unset it and the nightly's first job is skipped. NIGHTLY_ARCHES narrows the matrix, resolved most-specific-first: workflow_dispatch input, then the variable, then ARCHES in the Makefile.

Start at one architecture: three simultaneous failures are three times the log for one cause and, at roughly $14 an arch, triple the bill.

docs.title: The Nightly
docs.text:
.github/workflows/nightly.yml runs at 02:17 UTC, one job per architecture, each calling .builders/nightly.sh on a CodeBuild machine. A GitHub-hosted job collects the reports, comments on one nightly-labelled issue and publishes to data/nightly/. It skips itself when main has not moved since the last successful scheduled run — an unchanged tree is a bill with no result.

nightly.sh is deliberately not perfrun.sh: a rented machine has no balance.sh over ssh, no journalctl -u zot, so it times bake invocations and claims nothing more.

The schedule is warm-only, and warm — registry cache live — is what publishes. A cold run pushes nothing and deletes its own sccache prefix: a measurement for roughly double the bill, via -f run_cold=true. When both run, cold goes first, or it reads what the warm build wrote.

docs.title: Cache Errors Are Reported Separately From The Exit Code
docs.text: Every cache-to carries ignore-error=true, so a rejected export cannot fail an otherwise good build — but a night where every export failed exits 0 with the next warm build secretly cold. The report counts them separately: a green nightly with a climbing cache-error count is the failure mode to watch.

docs.title: Where The Warmth Lives
docs.text:
Nothing on the machine survives the build. Two caches do.

The registry cache is what makes a warm build warm. rocm-bake.hcl carries 39 type=registry,mode=max refs — every intermediate layer, not just the final image's — which the next night imports from ECR. Hence no docker pull $REPO:nightly plus --cache-from: a single-image cache does strictly less.

sccache on S3 is the object cache. A rented machine cannot reach the fleet's WebDAV endpoint, so the nightly sets SCCACHE_BUCKET, which outranks SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT in the Dockerfiles; an empty value counts as unset, so the same bake file serves the fleet.

LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE is free and worth enabling, but rarely survives a 24-hour gap. The S3 zip cache must not be used for layers: target-costs totals 17.6 GB per run, and shipping that around every build is the bottleneck the registry cache avoids.

Two settings are not handled by the setup script. nightly.sh --ensure-ecr creates missing repositories first — ECR does not create one on push the way Zot does, and the failure lands at the end of a long build — so the role needs ecr:CreateRepository. And set REGISTRY_INSECURE=false: the bake file defaults it true for the fleet's plain-HTTP Zot, and left that way against ECR every cache export fails, hidden by ignore-error=true.

A full run is measured at $13.94 for thirteen targets on one architecture, with zero cache errors. See Building on AWS.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Failures that have actually happened here, with the line that identifies each one.

docs.title: Connection Refused
docs.text:
systemctl status zot              # bare metal, not a container
sudo journalctl -u zot -n 50
curl -s http://snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/v2/_catalog
make zot-check

docs.title: Two Failures That Look Similar From A Build Log
docs.text:
Log line Cause no such host The builder cannot resolve the tailnet name. It was created without --driver-opt network=host, so Docker gave it the upstream resolver instead of the host's MagicDNS one. http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client DNS is fine but the client will not speak plain HTTP. For the Docker daemon, check insecure-registries in /etc/docker/daemon.json; for BuildKit, confirm the builder was created from the fleet manifest with make builder-<node> rather than by hand — a builder created with no --config has no [registry] block.

Both settings are fixed at builder-create time, so the fix is always docker buildx rm <name> then make builder-<name> — editing the toml does nothing to an existing builder. If pushes get 401, docker login as ci.

docs.title: Push Dies At Exactly 60 Seconds
docs.text:
Zot's default HTTP read timeout is 60 s, measured across the whole request body. The ROCm base image has a single 8.67 GB layer, which cannot cross a 1 Gb/s link in under ~73 s, so every push failed at the 60 s mark. The client-side error is a connection reset, which reads like a network fault; the giveaway is Zot's own log:

PUT /v2/.../blobs/uploads/...  statusCode: 500  latency: "1m0s"
error: "read tcp ...: i/o timeout"   Content-Length: 8672333352

/etc/zot/config.json needs "readTimeout": "30m" and "writeTimeout": "30m" under "http", then a restart; that layer then pushes in ~200 s. Zot is deployed from outside this repository, so the setting belongs in whatever provisions it, or it reverts.

docs.title: The Compiler Cache
docs.text:
The build refuses to start when the store is unreachable, so a silent no-cache build should not happen. If it does:

make cache-summary    # endpoint, size, disk, deltas and hit rates
make cache-check      # can every node reach it?
make cache-logs       # the WebDAV access log

Run cache-summary twice a minute apart during a build — the interval line is the one that matters. The hit-rate column comes from the telemetry textfile, not the store: WebDAV has no stats verb.

docs.title: Three Failure Modes With Distinct Signatures
docs.text:
Log line Cause No such file or directory on a source path The client reached a server outside its own container. Structurally impossible now that the server is addressed over a unix socket, but this is what it looked like. cache storage failed to read … I/O error The store's address did not resolve. Check the [dns] block in .builders/buildkitd.toml.in, and that the Makefile resolved WEBDAV_IP — build containers address the store by IP, not by name. Cache write errors climbing The store's filesystem is full. make cache-summary shows the disk line.

SCCACHE_LOG=debug reveals what sccache's "Cache errors" counter is counting; it is not the default because debug logs every lookup, and a cold Triton does 361 of them. After changing the buildkitd config: docker buildx rm snoc-strix && make builder-snoc-strix.

docs.title: "HIP Not Found"
docs.text:
rocm-smi --showversion     # are the ROCm modules loaded?
ls -la /dev/kfd /dev/dri   # is the GPU visible?

Compiling for an architecture does not need a GPU; this matters only for make test and make gpu-test.

docs.title: A Build Fails At The Last Target, Every Time
docs.text: pytorch-test has found its way into a group. It cannot run inside the build graph: its stage exits 1 when torch.cuda.is_available() is false, and a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd. Use make test.

docs.title: AITER's Wheel Build Exits 1 After ~51 Minutes
docs.text: On RDNA. Every kernel compiles and the build then fails in the JIT module phase: six of 68 modules carry CDNA-only code and setup.py treats a failure as fatal. The default is level 0 everywhere, so this means PREBUILD_KERNELS has been pinned to 2 — a pin only safe on CDNA. See Multiple GFX targets.

docs.title: A Build Is Wedged
docs.text:
make build-stop        # cancel builds started from this repo
make builder-restart   # restart buildkitd on $(BUILDER)

builder-restart drops that node's in-memory build state. The registry layer cache and the shared compiler cache are untouched, so the next build still picks up where it can.
