A build cancelled by build-stop is recorded by BuildKit as Error with no detail, indistinguishable from a real failure. make build-watch reads a stop file so it can label those correctly.

docs.title: Alternating Architectures Are Both Always Cold
docs.text: Fixed by CACHE_ARCH; if it recurs, check that the target actually scopes its cache ref by architecture. triton-wheel deliberately does not, because it compiles no device code.

docs.title: Insufficient Disk Space
docs.text:
docker system df
docker system prune -a

Remember the BuildKit store is bounded by gckeepstorage = "100GB" per node and is shared with the other project on these builders.

docs.title: No Metrics Appeared
docs.text:
./telemetry/build.sh --builder snoc-strix pytorch   # run it directly
docker buildx history ls --builder snoc-strix       # is there history to read?

Metrics land in telemetry/out/ when the node_exporter directory is not writable — the wrapper says so. sccache counters are absent when a target was fully layer-cached: the build step never ran, so it printed no stats.

docs.title: A Frozen Run Is Recorded As frozen*
docs.text: The registry eviction was refused, so the run was really cold — Zot needs deletes enabled. Such rows are excluded from every published ratio.

docs.title: The Harness Exits Immediately Saying A Build Is Running
docs.text: By design: two builds on one node contend for cores and memory. It exits 0 so it is safe to drive from cron; make build-status shows what is running.

docs.title: Results Look Implausible
docs.text: Check the job count: the same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32, and a ratio is only printed when both sides were measured at the same width. BENCH_MAX_JOBS pins it.

docs.title: The Endpoint Is Healthy But Nothing Is Cached
docs.text: /health is not evidence. Run make serve-test, which requires the second prefill of a repeated prefix to be measurably cheaper and reads LMCache's own log for the store and the retrieve.

docs.title: The Stack Fails At Startup
docs.text: Check HSA_ENABLE_IPC_MODE_LEGACY. It decides whether the two containers can share KV memory at all, and no amount of TRANSFER_MODE tuning will work around it.

docs.title: A Pull Fails Naming A Plausible-Looking Tag
docs.text: The serving tag comes from GPU_HOST's architecture, not the build default — make list-vars prints the resolved SERVE_ARCH. If the host is unreachable it falls back to the build architecture, which may be an image nobody has built.

docs.title: import torchvision Fails
docs.text:
This should no longer happen: torchvision-wheel builds torchvision against this torch and Dockerfile.vllm installs it. If it does, the ROCm wheel has been replaced by PyPI's CUDA build somewhere — check what is actually installed:

python -c "import torchvision; print(torchvision.__version__)"

A version with no +rocm local segment is the CUDA wheel. /etc/pip-constraints.txt exists to make that resolution fail loudly rather than succeed, so also check that PIP_CONSTRAINT is still set in the container and that the constraints file still has a torchvision== line. See Serving stack.

docs.title: Everything Is Slow And Nothing Is Obviously Broken
docs.text:
In order:

  1. make builder-logs — a registry, DNS or cache fault shows up here while the build merely looks slow.
  2. make cache-summary, twice a minute apart. A flat object count during a compile means the compiler cache is not being written.
  3. make layer-summary — a target that moved nodes must refetch from the registry.
  4. make builder-load — something else may be on the node.

docs.title: Build Performance
docs.text:
Two harnesses, answering different questions.

This page is bench.sh: one target at a time, four cache conditions, an isolated compiler cache. It answers what does this target cost, and its numbers are comparable run to run.

Instrumented fleet runs is make perf-cold: every wheel at once, across all three nodes, with CPU, cache and registry traffic sampled throughout. It answers what does a full cold build look like, and its numbers are throughput under contention.

A third lane, the nightly on AWS, times two bake invocations on one rented machine. Do not quote a number from any of them as if it came from another.

docs.title: The Four Cache Conditions
docs.text:
Measured rather than estimated. They nest: each is the one below it with a further cache taken away.

flowchart LR
    frozen["<b>frozen</b><br/>nothing, anywhere"] --> cold["<b>cold</b><br/>base image local"]
    cold --> warm["<b>warm</b><br/>caches populated,<br/>new commit"]
    warm --> hot["<b>hot</b><br/>same commit,<br/>everything cached"]

docs.title: Frozen
docs.text:
Cold, and Zot holds no pull-through copy of the upstream base image either, so its layers egress from Docker Hub. The ROCm base is a single 8.67 GB layer, so the difference between frozen and cold is essentially WAN bandwidth — the number to quote when someone asks what the local registry is worth.

make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=frozen BUILDER=snoc-think

frozen is destructive and is not in the nightly rotation

It deletes Zot's cached manifest for the upstream base and runs docker buildx prune -af on the target node, emptying that node's content store including any other project's layers. BENCH_FROZEN_PRUNE=0 skips the prune. If Zot refuses the delete, the run is shown as frozen* and excluded from every published ratio rather than averaged in.

docs.title: Cold
docs.text:
No layer cache, no compiler cache, but the base image is resident in Zot. What a new build node, or a changed base image, costs. The upper bound on compile cost.

--no-cache alone is not cold: sccache would still serve every object from the shared store and the build would finish in minutes while measuring nothing. The harness also sets FORCE_RECACHE and isolates the run under its own SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX.

make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold
make build-cold COLD_TARGET=pytorch   # the same conditions, outside the harness

docs.title: Warm
docs.text:
Layer and compiler caches are populated, but SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH moved — which is what every new commit does. The case that matters day to day.

Under the current design that costs nothing, and the result is the assertion rather than the number: if warm ever diverges from hot, some per-commit value has found its way back into an image digest. That has happened twice. See Reproducibility.

docs.title: Hot
docs.text: Same commit, everything cached. The lower bound, and mostly a check that the caches are read at all. The harness distinguishes two kinds when it computes ratios: one where the compile ran and sccache served every object, and one where BuildKit skipped the step outright.

docs.title: Measured Results
docs.text: Medians, keyed by target, builder, architecture and job count. Both architecture and job count are in the key because both are dominant variables: the same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32, and vLLM's kernel prebuild is about 50 minutes on gfx950 against hours on gfx1201. Cold on one architecture over hot on another is not a ratio. See Methodology.

docs.title: Every Run
docs.text: Each point is one build. The spread is real and large — PyTorch's hot time varies about threefold run to run — which is why the tables above quote medians and print n beside them.

docs.title: Reproducing This
docs.text:
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold BUILDER=snoc-think   # one scenario
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=all                       # cold, warm, hot
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=everything                # and frozen first
make bench-report                                   # render as markdown

The harness refuses to run while a real build is in flight on the target builder — two builds on one node contend for cores and memory. It exits 0 rather than failing, so it is safe to drive from cron. Results accumulate as JSON lines in /var/tmp/rocm-bench/results.jsonl.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
The numbers on this page come from a file on the gh-pages branch, not from the repository. Nothing in main carries benchmark data.

make bench-data              # aggregate into dist/bench/bench.json
make bench-publish PUSH=1    # commit it onto gh-pages and push
make perf-publish PUSH=1     # the newest instrumented fleet run

Instrumented fleet runs land at data/perf/, which opens on the newest run and offers every published run in a selector; each run keeps a permalink of the form data/perf/<stamp>/. The nightly lands at data/nightly/, written by CI rather than from a build node.

Those links point at the selector root rather than a stamp, which is correct for exactly one run, and they are absolute because data/ lives on gh-pages and never in the docs source — a relative link would be a broken internal link to mkdocs --strict.

Perf runs publish from a build node because that is the only place the data exists. The docs workflow preserves data/ when it deploys.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: .builders/bench.sh is the harness. It runs one make build-* per measurement, parses the build log, and appends a JSON line. Everything below is a correction to something that produced a wrong number first.

docs.title: What A Run Records
docs.text:
{
  "ts": "2026-10-20T02:00:00+00:00",
  "scenario": "cold",
  "target": "pytorch",
  "builder": "snoc-think",
  "arch": "gfx950",
  "seconds": 2342,
  "rc": 0,
  "steps_cached": 0,
  "steps_total": 11,
  "sccache_requests": 5674,
  "sccache_hits": 0,
  "max_jobs": 10,
  "node_load_at_start": 0.4,
  "node_load_at_end": 12.0,
  "registry_evicted": null,
  "failure": null
}

A failing build is a result and the harness never aborts on one; failure carries the first line that looks like a cause rather than the generic wrapper. log is stripped before publication.

docs.title: Guards Before A Run
docs.text:
Is the node busy? The harness asks buildx what the builder is solving, not the process table — pgrep -f matched the script's own invoker, and was fleet-wide besides.

Has memory settled? MAX_JOBS is derived from MemAvailable when the compile step starts. Launching straight after another benchmark samples it while BuildKit is still flushing layers: one cold PyTorch derived MAX_JOBS=3 on a node that reported 18 GB free two minutes later. The harness polls until two readings agree.

That is necessary but not sufficient, because the build's own earlier steps have taken memory by then — a cold PyTorch that settled at 21 GB derived 5, where the same node gives a hot run 10. So cold and hot are measured at different job counts by construction. BENCH_MAX_JOBS pins it when the point is to compare scenarios.

docs.title: Parsing The Log
docs.text: Two numbers come out of the build log, and both were wrong at first.

docs.title: Steps Cached
docs.text:
A step is a vertex BuildKit labels [n/m], and cached means that vertex reported CACHED — not the telemetry wrapper's count, which includes loading the Dockerfile, metadata and exporting among the total, none of which can ever be cached.

The vertex name carries a bake-target prefix whenever the build has more than one target, and pytorch always does now: [pytorch builder 4/11] against a single-target build's bare [builder 9/11]. An earlier regex allowed only the bare form, so a PyTorch benchmark counted zero of zero.

docs.title: sccache Counters
docs.text:
Not from ^Cache hits — the lines carry a BuildKit prefix (#32 178.7 Cache hits 5674), so that anchor never matched. And not from the telemetry summary, the first fix and also wrong: a PyTorch build prints two stats blocks, its own and Triton's, and the wrapper attributed Triton's to both.

BuildKit carries the association in the step number: #32 [pytorch builder 10/11] RUN … ties step 32 to pytorch, and every stats line from that step is prefixed #32.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
frozen and cold runs set SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX to a per-run value and delete it afterwards, so they never pollute the shared cache.

cache-to is cleared for every run: the credential helper fails outside an interactive session. Reads are anonymous and still work, so cache hits are faithful; what these numbers exclude is push time.

docs.title: Forcing A Recompile
docs.text:
BENCH_FORCE_COMPILE=1 writes an HCL override setting no-cache-filter = ["builder"]. It must arrive as an override file: bake accepts the attribute there, but --set target.no-cache-filter= is silently dropped (buildx 0.30.1). The older method — bumping MAX_JOBS to a value it had not had — conflated the cache-buster with the variable under test.

It invalidates every step in the stage, not just the compile. Whether that changes the timing is not established: the pin-change method spans 203–617 s and contains the forced range entirely.

docs.title: How The Ratios Are Computed
docs.text:
Three pools, keyed by (target, builder, arch, max_jobs):

Pool Which Rows frozen scenario == "frozen" and the registry eviction succeeded cold scenario == "cold" compiled scenario == "hot" where under half the steps were cached skipped scenario == "hot" where at least half were cached

and three ratios:

  • registry — frozen ÷ cold. What Zot's pull-through is worth.
  • compiler cache — cold ÷ compiled. sccache served the requests instead of the compiler.
  • layer cache — compiled ÷ skipped. BuildKit skipped the compile step outright, so sccache saw no requests at all.

Dividing cold by whichever hot run came last conflated the last two and once printed "2297.3x" — a cold run against a 3 s layer-cache hit that compiled nothing. Whether the compile ran is judged on steps cached, not on sccache having reported anything: rows from before the parser was fixed carry requests=0 because nothing was recorded.

docs.title: Which Sample
docs.text: The markdown report quotes the most recent run at a key. The minimum picks an outlier and biases the ratio in opposite directions on each side; the median assumes one population, and this pipeline changed underneath its own measurements. A ratio answers what the cache buys now, so the newest sample is the right estimator, with n and the observed range beside it. The charts use medians, because a chart shows a distribution over time.

docs.title: Why Job Count And Architecture Are In The Key
docs.text:
Both are dominant parameters, not nuisance ones. The same cold PyTorch is 6892 s at 5 jobs and 2342 s at 32, and vLLM's kernel prebuild is about 50 minutes on gfx950 against hours on gfx1201. Pooling across either coordinate produces an average of nothing.

The harness resolves the architecture through make rather than a literal. Rows from before the field existed read as gfx950. A ratio is printed only when both sides were measured at the same width and architecture.

docs.title: Contamination
docs.text: The builders are shared with another project. Load average is recorded at the start and the end, because one sample at t=0 does not characterise a twenty-minute run: the slowest cold Triton on record, 1168 s against a 432–669 s cluster, began at load 0.99 and finished with the node at 41 on 32 cores. Contention arriving after the start is the best candidate for the spread these numbers carry.

docs.title: Instrumented Fleet Runs
docs.text: Every wheel built across the whole fleet at once, with CPU, memory, compiler-cache and registry traffic sampled throughout. Published at data/perf/.

docs.title: Three Harnesses, Three Questions
docs.text:
bench.sh make perf-cold make perf-warm runs targets one at a time across the fleet at once across the fleet at once caches isolated none both, as normal answers what does this target cost a full cold build the build you actually run numbers are isolated per-target throughput under contention throughput under contention

Do not quote a number from one as if it came from another

bench.sh serialises on purpose and isolates its compiler cache. The perf-* harnesses run the fleet flat out, so three builds share the sccache store and the registry — both on Strix, which is also a build node. The nightly on AWS is a fourth lane again.

A warm run's cost is almost entirely export rather than compute.

docs.title: Running One
docs.text:
make perf-plan                      # placement only, builds nothing
make perf-cold PERF_ARCH=gfx1201    # cold: no caches, hours
make perf-warm PERF_ARCH=gfx1201    # warm: caches on, pushes
make perf-report                    # markdown + SVG from the newest run
make perf-serve                     # live chart on :8090

Cold means --no-cache and an sccache prefix of its own: a cold run must not evict the fleet's working cache, and must not hit it either. PERF_ARCH, PERF_TARGETS and PERF_BIND configure the rest.

perf-serve binds every interface

The usual viewer is a laptop on the LAN that is not on tailscale. What that exposes is build telemetry — hostnames, CPU figures, step names — with no credentials and no registry access.

docs.title: Bootstrapping, And The Cold Namespace
docs.text:
Neither harness builds the images its wheels sit on, so they bootstrap themselves: depgraph.py --missing-targets names what the registry lacks, and those are built and pushed before the measured run. That step is warm and pushed even under perf-cold, and is not sampled — cold is a claim about the wheels being measured, not their inputs.

perf-cold pushes into ${REGISTRY_NAME}-coldrun. It used to pass --no-push while balance.sh set PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 — which it must, since target: contexts only resolve within one builder — so every target resolved its inputs from the previous run. REGISTRY_NAME moves tags, caches and PUB_* refs together, so a fresh namespace builds the whole stack from nothing and the live one is never written to. PERF_COLD_NAMESPACE= keeps two cold runs apart.

docs.title: What A Run Collects
docs.text:
Into /var/tmp/rocm-perf/<stamp>/:

File From Answers samples.jsonl node_exporter, polled CPU, memory, disk and network over time trace-<target>.json the builder's build record what ran, when, for how long sccache.log the WebDAV nginx log, sliced what was written to the compiler cache zot.jsonl Zot's structured log, sliced layer-cache and image writes, with sizes artifacts.txt wheelhouse.py what ended up published index.html + data.json perfreport.py the interactive chart and its sidecar

The two cache logs are appended to during the run, then replaced by a single authoritative slice at the end — without that a run in flight had no cache data, and the chart drops the whole bar lane when hits is missing. Appending beats re-slicing because zot.jsonl reached 294.6 MB on one run, costing 6 s per perf-serve regen; that parse, not the capture, sets the refresh floor.

perf-report writes report.md with SVG charts, plus an index.html with overlaid CPU and memory lines, a legend filtering by builder and target, and per-band hover showing the RUN commands a phase covers. Both share one axis because both are percentages — a second y-scale would make it a dual-axis chart, the form that misleads most reliably — so memory is distinguished by dash and colour keeps following the builder. perf-serve polls data.json rather than reloading, because the legend is the filter.

make perf-publish PUSH=1 puts that page on the web with a selector for every earlier run.

docs.title: build And total Are Different Numbers
docs.text:
build is the span of the target's own steps; total is the whole record. The gap is setup plus export, usually the larger.

In cold mode the export is excluded. --no-push suppresses the image push but not the cache export, a separate registry write, so perfrun.sh clears it with --set *.cache-to=:

On one gfx1201 run triton-wheel reported 38m52s, of which the trace accounted for 15m48s. The other 23m04s — 59% of its headline duration — was uploading mode=max cache.

In warm mode the export is the point. perftrace.py keeps BuildKit's HTTP PUT/POST spans alongside the step spans, banded as upload. They were discarded until a triton-wheel run showed 92 s of steps inside a 430 s record — a node that looked idle was uploading 6.4 GB.

docs.title: Dependency Ordering, Not Stage Barriers
docs.text:
A target starts when every dependency inside the run has finished and been pushed; everything else is resolved from Zot and checked by preflight. Stage barriers ordered work correctly but idled whole nodes:

On one gfx1201 run stage 1 took 44m16s of wall clock to do 77m09s of work, leaving 55m39s of idle builder time, with the weakest node idle for 82% of it.

Flat per-node queues recovered that time but could not express a dependency at all — which is how a gfx1250 run scheduled vllm-wheel against a pytorch image nothing was building.

PERF_TARGETS defaults to the wheels group plus pytorch, which is not a wheel but is the most expensive target in the graph and the image every wheel builds FROM.

docs.title: What A Target Costs Depends On Which Node Runs It
docs.text:
Two terms from .builders/target-costs, which describes targets, and one from the fleet manifest, which describes machines:

build <target> <seconds>   compile cost, roughly node-independent
cache <target> <bytes>     what the target transfers when it exports
link_mbps: <MB/s>          that node's upload throughput to the store

Cost is build + cache/link_mbps, and the packer picks the node that finishes soonest, not the one least loaded. The second term is not a refinement: uplinks span a factor of 25, so the same 6.4 GB export is about a minute on one node and 28 on another.

Ranking on build time alone sent triton-wheel, the largest export of any target, to the only node behind WiFi. Moving it to a wired node took it from 25m25s to 7m09s.

On a fleet whose nodes share one uplink speed the term cancels and placement collapses to plain LPT.

Warm runs can invert which node is critical, since every build term collapses towards zero while the cache terms stay:

In one perf-warm run pytorch-wheel was a cache hit and freed its node after 55 s, leaving the WiFi node's four small targets — 2.8 GB between them — as the critical path of a 26-minute run.

Queues are fixed at plan time, so nothing migrates once packed.

Take the byte figures from a normal run

A cold run passes --no-push, so its export counts the cache but not the image — which under-counted aiter-wheel by 4.3×.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: Several of those streams are produced by one file and parsed by another with nothing but a comment connecting them: an nginx log_format and a regex, the balancer's placement line and the report's parser, target-costs and the packer. Every one fails the same way — the producer changes, the consumer silently matches nothing, and the report renders perfectly while saying 0. .builders/check-contracts.py asserts each pair still agrees, reading files only, in under a second.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Every build records its own metrics. Separate from the benchmark harness: telemetry runs on every build including real ones, the harness runs under controlled conditions.

telemetry/build.sh wraps a bake invocation and writes Prometheus metrics for each target it produced, exiting with bake's own status — a drop-in replacement for a bare bake. Every make build-* and push-* already routes through it.

./telemetry/build.sh --builder snoc-think pytorch
make build-pytorch                   # the same thing
TELEMETRY=0 make build-pytorch       # a bare bake

Both data sources already exist, so nothing is instrumented and no collector daemon runs: BuildKit's history API for duration, status and cached-step count, and sccache's own stats, printed at the end of the build step and scraped out of the replayed log — they cannot be queried afterwards, since the server dies with the build container.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Eight per-target gauges, labelled {target="…",builder="…"}:

Metric Meaning rocm_build_duration_seconds BuildKit-reported duration rocm_build_steps_total Steps in the build rocm_build_steps_cached How many came from the layer cache rocm_build_layer_cache_hit_ratio Cached steps over total rocm_build_target_success 1 if the target completed rocm_build_sccache_hits Compiler-cache hits for that build rocm_build_sccache_misses Compiler-cache misses rocm_build_sccache_hit_ratio Hits over hits plus misses

Three more describe the invocation as a whole, labelled {builder="…"}: rocm_build_invocation_duration_seconds, rocm_build_invocation_success and rocm_build_last_run_timestamp_seconds.

A HELP/TYPE block is emitted only when at least one sample exists for that name, so a scrape never sees a declared-but-empty metric.

docs.title: Where It Lands
docs.text:
/var/lib/node_exporter/textfile_collector/rocm_pytorch_build.prom

Written to a temp path and renamed, so the collector never reads a partial file, and picked up by the node_exporter already on :9100. When that directory is not writable the wrapper falls back to telemetry/out/ and says so.

docs.title: Attributing sccache Stats To A Target
docs.text:
The subtle part. Replayed history records carry no bake-target prefix on their vertex headers, so the step cannot be identified the way the harness does it live. Each Dockerfile tees its stats to a known file instead, and the wrapper finds the vertex whose command contains that marker:

Target Marker pytorch /opt/pytorch/sccache-stats.txt triton-wheel /wheels-triton-sccache-stats.txt aiter-wheel /wheels-aiter-sccache-stats.txt torchvision-wheel /wheels-torchvision-sccache-stats.txt

Having found the step number, it reads that step's stats lines. With no marker present it falls back to the last stats block in the log, which is a guess and is why the markers exist.

docs.title: Reading It Back
docs.text:
make build-status     # build records on $(BUILDER), with the node each ran on
make build-inspect    # duration, steps, cached steps, VCS revision
make layer-summary    # layer reuse per image, most recent build of each
make cache-summary    # compiler-cache size and the delta since last call

layer-summary is keyed by image, not node: which node a target ran on is an artefact of scheduling, so a per-node view answers the wrong question. The node is still shown, because it explains a low number — a target that moved nodes cannot use the previous node's local BuildKit cache and must refetch from Zot.

docs.title: When Numbers Are Missing
docs.text: sccache counters are absent when a target was fully layer-cached: the build step never ran, so it printed no stats. That is correct, and it is exactly the distinction the harness uses to separate a hot run that compiled from one that skipped the compile.

docs.title: Bake Variables
docs.text: rocm-bake.hcl declares 52 variables and is the single source for every value a build reads. The Makefile parses the variable blocks at parse time and reads the defaults out, so make build-pytorch and a bare docker buildx bake pytorch always agree; check-defaults.py fails CI if they drift. make list-vars prints what is actually in effect, and is authoritative if this page has aged.

docs.title: Versions And Refs
docs.text:
Variable Default PYTORCH_VERSION 2.15.0 ROCM_VERSION 10.1.0-full PYTHON_VERSION 3.14 TRITON_VERSION 3.9.0 TRITON_REF aad2a60d958f945420c5c40936b37d411fb02e89 AITER_REF v0.1.28 TORCHVISION_REF v0.29.2 ATOM_REF v0.1.9 NIXL_REF v1.5.2 UCX_REF v1.22.0 VLLM_REF v0.33.0 CUPY_REF v14.2.0 LMCACHE_REF v0.5.6 RUST_VERSION 1.95 GIT_REF "" - a specific PyTorch ref to build

This table is generated from rocm-bake.hcl by make version-scrub, and make version-scrub-check fails CI if it drifts. make version-check compares each of these against the latest upstream release and against the wheels published in the registry.

The four serving-stack refs are release tags, never branches. A moving ref would be served from the layer cache indefinitely once built, so an "update" would silently be a no-op.

RUST_VERSION tracks the channel in vLLM's rust-toolchain.toml, which v0.33 still pins to 1.95; setup.py builds vllm/vllm-rs.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
Variable Default REGISTRY snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 REGISTRY_NAME rocm-pytorch REGISTRY_INSECURE true SOURCE_URL https://github.com/sbates130272/rocm-pytorch-build

REGISTRY_INSECURE is true for the fleet's Zot, which serves plain HTTP on a tailnet. Set it false for any registry with TLS and auth — ECR, GHCR, Docker Hub. It reaches the registry.insecure= field of every cache-from and cache-to in the file, and leaving it true against an HTTPS registry fails the cache export rather than falling back, which ignore-error=true then swallows.

docs.title: Architecture And Build Shape
docs.text:
Variable Default PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH gfx950 Semicolon-separated list; a list produces one fat binary USE_AITER ON USE_FLYDSL ON USE_FLASH_ATTENTION ON USE_ROCM_CK_SDPA_GFX12 "" RDNA4 Composable Kernel SDPA, new in PyTorch 2.15 and OFF upstream. ON takes effect only on a gfx12 RDNA4 target; anywhere else it stays OFF MAX_JOBS "" Empty derives it per node from MemAvailable PREBUILD_KERNELS "" Empty means 0, on every architecture. Level 2 builds no wheel at all on gfx1201 or gfx125x ROCM_PRUNE_PROFILE keep-toolchain How hard docker/rocm-prune.sh cuts the ROCm SDK down. minimal also drops the headers and the HIP cmake package — see Image sizes

The prebuild level no longer derives from the architecture; it is 0 everywhere unless pinned. See Multiple GFX targets for what the architecture still does decide.

docs.title: Compiler Cache
docs.text: Variable Default SCCACHE_WEBDAV_HOST snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net The nginx WebDAV store SCCACHE_WEBDAV_PORT 8081 SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT "" Composed from host and port; the Makefile supplies a resolved address SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX rocm-pytorch Namespace within the store SCCACHE_BUCKET "" S3 store, for builds off the fleet. Empty selects WebDAV SCCACHE_REGION "" Required whenever SCCACHE_BUCKET is set SCCACHE_S3_KEY_PREFIX rocm-pytorch Namespace within the bucket SCCACHE_LOG warn debug reveals what "Cache errors" is counting SCCACHE_VERSION 0.19.0 0.8.0 is the floor for caching hipcc -x hip REQUIRE_SCCACHE 1 Refuse to compile when the store is unreachable

docs.title: WebDAV On The Fleet, S3 Off It
docs.text:
The WebDAV store is nginx on the services node, reached over the tailnet; a rented machine has neither, so it needs a store that outlives it — hence S3. See Building on AWS.

The two coexist. sccache ranks S3 above WebDAV and treats an empty SCCACHE_BUCKET as unset, so the S3 variables are inert on SNOC. Verified against sccache 0.19.0: unset and "" both select WebDAV, a non-empty bucket selects S3.

Credentials are not variables. They reach the build as a BuildKit secret mounted for the life of the instruction, so they never become a build arg and never land in image history or a published tag:

aws configure export-credentials --format env-no-export > /tmp/awscreds
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.secrets=id=aws,src=/tmp/awscreds' \
  cupy-wheel
shred -u /tmp/awscreds

A readable-but-unwritable bucket caches nothing, silently

REQUIRE_SCCACHE=1 catches bad credentials and a missing bucket — sccache probes at server start and aborts. What it cannot catch is a policy granting reads but not writes. Grant s3:ListBucket too: without it a missing key returns 403 rather than 404, and the probe fails for the wrong reason.

Session credentials expire

Credentials from the environment carry no expiry hint for sccache to refresh against, so a build longer than the session turns every later cache operation into a 403 after the preflight passed. Prefer an sts:assume-role with an explicit long --duration-seconds.

| FORCE_RECACHE | false | true recompiles everything, ignoring sccache |

There is deliberately no SCCACHE_SERVER_PORT

Build containers reach their sccache server over a unix socket, because the builders run with network=host and a fixed port would be shared fleet-wide. See Caching.

Setting SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT yourself only affects a bare bake — the Makefile exports its own resolved form unconditionally.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Variable Default SDE_EPOCH 1700000000 SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pinned into every image config SDE_BASE … SDE_TORCHVISION "" Per-image overrides; empty means use SDE_EPOCH VCS_REF "" Supplied by the Makefile; gets a -dirty suffix BUILD_DATE "" Supplied by the Makefile as the commit's own timestamp

The eleven per-image variables are SDE_ROCM, SDE_BASE, SDE_PYTORCH, SDE_TRITON, SDE_AITER, SDE_RUNTIME, SDE_NIXL, SDE_VLLM, SDE_LMCACHE, SDE_CUPY and SDE_TORCHVISION. See Reproducibility for why the epoch is a constant.

docs.title: Caching And Scheduling
docs.text: Variable Default CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX "" Empty writes the rolling tag; -ref refreshes the frozen baseline PUBLISHED_INPUTS "" 1 resolves sibling inputs from the registry instead of target: contexts RUN_ID dev Stamped into every BuildKit history record name

docs.title: Overriding Without Editing
docs.text:
# A different PyTorch version
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.PYTORCH_VERSION=2.13.0" pytorch

# A different ROCm base
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.ROCM_VERSION=7.14" pytorch

# A different registry
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.REGISTRY=myregistry.com:5000" \
  --set "*.args.REGISTRY_NAME=rocm-pytorch" pytorch

# A specific PyTorch ref
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.GIT_REF=refs/heads/develop" pytorch

# Build even though the compiler cache is unreachable
docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl \
  --set "*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0" pytorch

--set on a bake variable is not the same as on an arg

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT, SCCACHE_LOG, PUBLISHED_INPUTS, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* family are bake variables read from the environment. Using --set '*.args.X=…' for one of them adds the arg to every target and changes their cache keys. Use the environment:

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT=http://other-host:8081 \
  docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl pytorch

Through the Makefile, BAKE_EXTRA passes arbitrary flags to any target:

make build-pytorch BAKE_EXTRA='--set pytorch.args.SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=1700000001'

docs.title: Build Targets And Tags
docs.text:
Sixteen targets. Every published repository is under snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/, elided below.

Each target emits three tags: a versioned one, :latest, and an immutable -g<sha> tag whenever VCS_REF is non-empty.

Target Repository Versioned tag rocm-runtime rocm-runtime ${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} pytorch-src pytorch-src ${PYTORCH_VERSION} (no arch, no ROCm) pytorch-base base ${ROCM_VERSION}-${PYTHON_VERSION}-${ARCH} pytorch pytorch ${PYTORCH_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} pytorch-wheel pytorch-wheel ${PYTORCH_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} pytorch-run runtime ${PYTORCH_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} pytorch-test pytorch ${PYTORCH_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH}-test triton-wheel triton-wheel ${TRITON_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION} aiter-wheel aiter-wheel ${PYTORCH_VERSION}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} torchvision-wheel torchvision-wheel ${TORCHVISION_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} cupy-wheel cupy-wheel ${CUPY_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} nixl-wheel nixl-wheel ${NIXL_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} vllm vllm ${VLLM_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} vllm-wheel vllm-wheel ${VLLM_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} lmcache lmcache ${LMCACHE_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH} lmcache-wheel lmcache-wheel ${LMCACHE_REF}-${ROCM_VERSION}-${ARCH}

With the current defaults that resolves to:

rocm-runtime:10.1.0-full-gfx950
base:10.1.0-full-3.14-gfx950
pytorch-src:2.15.0
pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
pytorch-wheel:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
runtime:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
triton-wheel:3.9.0-10.1.0-full
aiter-wheel:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
torchvision-wheel:v0.29.2-10.1.0-full-gfx950
cupy-wheel:v14.2.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
nixl-wheel:v1.5.2-10.1.0-full-gfx950
vllm:v0.33.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
vllm-wheel:v0.33.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950
lmcache:v0.5.6-10.1.0-full-gfx950
lmcache-wheel:v0.5.6-10.1.0-full-gfx950

make zot-tags REPO=rocm-pytorch/pytorch lists what is actually published.

docs.title: Three Tags That Are Not What You Would Guess
docs.text:
triton-wheel carries no architecture and is version-prefixed. Triton is a compiler and publishes one noarch wheel, so the tag is 3.9.0-10.1.0-full. wheelhouse.py parses it without a gfx component.

pytorch-run publishes to runtime, with the architecture. It compiles nothing and takes no PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH, but it COPYs the torch wheel out of pytorch, so what it ships is as architecture-specific as that wheel. Without the architecture in the tag a gfx1201 runtime overwrote the gfx950 one.

base carries the architecture now, and did not used to. It builds FROM rocm-runtime, which holds kernel libraries for one card only, so the apt and pip layers on top are architecture-independent while what is underneath them is not. Without the architecture in the tag a gfx950 base would overwrite a gfx1201 one exactly as runtime once did.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Group Members default rocm-runtime, pytorch-src, pytorch-base, pytorch, pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel wheels pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, nixl-wheel, torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, vllm-wheel, lmcache-wheel serving torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel

There is no all group. pytorch-test and pytorch-run are deliberately outside default — why. wheels is separate because each of its members builds FROM an image that must already be published, so the group cannot run against a cold registry. WHEEL_REPOS in the Makefile must match it; check-defaults.py fails CI if it drifts.

docs.title: Dockerfiles
docs.text:
Every Dockerfile lives in docker/, and the build context is always the repository root.

File Produces Dockerfile.base pytorch-base Dockerfile.pytorch pytorch, pytorch-wheel, pytorch-test Dockerfile.runtime pytorch-run Dockerfile.triton triton-wheel Dockerfile.aiter aiter-wheel Dockerfile.torchvision torchvision-wheel Dockerfile.cupy cupy-wheel Dockerfile.nixl nixl-wheel Dockerfile.vllm vllm, vllm-wheel Dockerfile.lmcache lmcache, lmcache-wheel

A wheel target is the same Dockerfile built to its wheel stage, which is why each *-wheel inherits from its image target.

docs.title: Image Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    up["rocm/dev-ubuntu-26.04:10.1.0-full"] --> base
    base["<b>base</b><br/>+ Python 3.14<br/>+ dev tools<br/>+ sccache client"]
    base --> pt["<b>pytorch</b><br/>built from source<br/>+ HIP/ROCm<br/>+ our triton wheel"]
    pt --> rt["<b>runtime</b><br/>torch wheel installed<br/>no build tools"]

docs.title: Cache Repositories
docs.text: Each target exports its layers to a *-cache repository, listed in Caching. make clean-cache removes only four of them, locally; the registry must be pruned separately.

docs.title: Image Sizes
docs.text: What each published image costs to pull, and which part is this project's doing. Numbers come from the Zot registry on the fleet; make image-publish pushes them onto gh-pages from the registry host.

docs.title: Shared, And Own
docs.text:
A layer digest under more than one repository is shared; the rest is that image's own, read from the manifests.

It is the only reading that is not misleading, because every run image descends from one common base: by total, vllm is the largest thing we build; by own, under a gigabyte. That base used to be rocm/dev-ubuntu-26.04, whose single layer is 8.67 GB — 71% to 95% of each published image.

own is the column to watch in review: total moving alone is a change to the base image, and own moving is one of ours.

docs.title: Wheels
docs.text:
The *-wheel targets publish scratch images holding one .whl each — what make fetch-torch-wheel and the pip index read, and why run images mount a wheel rather than copy it.

No split: one file shares nothing.

docs.title: Over Time
docs.text: One point per make image-data. Sizes move only when something is rebuilt, so the flat line is by design — a step in it is the event worth explaining.

docs.title: Layer Caches
docs.text:
Each build target exports its layer cache to a *-cache repository.

This table double-counts. The tags of one cache repo share most of their layers, so summing manifests is an upper bound — useful for comparing targets, useless as a disk figure.

They are bounded: each repo holds latest, latest-<arch> and latest-<arch>-ref per architecture in ARCHES, and every build overwrites the one it owns. Zot runs dedupe, gc and deleteUntagged itself.

Actual occupancy, from the host:

make zot-disk

docs.title: Regenerating
docs.text:
From the registry host, where the tailnet name resolves:

make image-sizes                      # the table, in the terminal
make image-sizes LAYERS=1             # with the per-layer breakdown
make image-sizes IMAGE_ARCH=gfx1201   # a card other than the default
make zot-disk                         # deduplicated disk, from the Zot host
make image-data                       # dist/images/images.json
make image-publish                    # commit it to gh-pages, locally
make image-publish PUSH=1             # and push

One architecture per table. shared counts a digest carried by more than one image in the set compared, so a table mixing cards reports shared layers as unshared and own comes out wrong.

image-publish reads the gh-pages copy first — the only place images.json's history exists.

docs.title: Why The Images Were The Size They Were
docs.text: Three things, in order of cost.

docs.title: The ROCm SDK Base — 7.13 GB
docs.text:
rocm/dev-ubuntu-26.04:10.1.0-full unpacks to 20.53 GB in one 8.67 GB layer: rocBLAS, hipBLASLt and MIOpen kernels for every architecture AMD supports, plus a full LLVM. Each image targets one architecture, and AMD publishes no -runtime variant.

rocm-runtime dpkg --purges the per-architecture packages for cards we do not target — ROCm 10.1 splits them as <component>10.1-<gfx> — 10.77 GB of the 20.53 alone:

removed how measured per-architecture packages (260 of them) dpkg --purge 10.77 GB static archives (*.a, 835 files) rm — with one exception 4.73 GB docs, man, info rm small /opt/rocm/lib/cmake rm — minimal only a few MB

A rm in a child layer reclaims nothing, so a second stage flattens it: COPY --from=pruned / / onto scratch — the whole root, not /opt/rocm, since an image missing ld.so.conf.d or the udev rules loads libamdhip64 and finds no device.

Measured, gfx1201: 8.67 GB → 1.42 GB, base adding 0.24 GB. An earlier 1.54 GB figure on gfx950 is withdrawn.

Two things the sweep must not remove

"Nothing loads a .a at run time" is true of the ROCm math libraries and false of the compiler's own runtime — clang links libclang_rt.builtins.a into every HIP compilation — and cmake's HIP detection reads hip-lang-config.cmake, which pytorch-wheel needs to build PyTorch here. Both were removed on reasoning about the runtime images, and both surfaced hours downstream as a failed wheel build naming neither ROCm nor the prune.

So Dockerfile.rocm-runtime compiles and links a real HIP program and checks the cmake package, in 0.9 s, at build time. Asserting files exist failed twice.

docker/rocm-prune.sh also asserts the kept architecture still has packages — else an image imports torch happily and has no kernels for its card.

docs.title: Prune Profiles
docs.text:
profile keeps for keep-toolchain (default) hipcc, the ROCm headers, LLVM, /opt/rocm/lib/cmake everything minimal none of them an image that compiles nothing

minimal is 0.4 GB better on a 4.4 GB tree, but giving pytorch-run its own would mean a second base image and a second layer cache per architecture — and the serving images need the toolchain anyway: AITER JIT-compiles on first use, Triton shells out to ld.lld.

amdrocm-rpp, amdrocm-rdc and amdrocm-rocshmem are 1.1 GB nothing here imports, kept because each is a hard Depends of the architecture core package: purging them leaves apt refusing every later operation downstream.

docs.title: Wheels Copied Into The Image That Installs Them — ~1.5 GB
docs.text: A COPY is a layer. Dockerfile.pytorch copied the torch wheel in (0.40 GB), installed it, then rm -rf in a later layer, so every pull paid for a wheel it could not use. Same for Triton (0.45 GB) and every wheel in the vLLM and LMCache images. All of those sites now use RUN --mount=type=bind,from=<stage>, so the wheel never becomes a layer; the *-wheel images still publish it.

docs.title: Dependencies That Cannot Run Here
docs.text:
The PyPI builds of torchvision, torchaudio and torchdata are CUDA builds, the only such thing here, and on ROCm their extensions fail to load. The optional-extras step that pulled them in carried || true and is gone from Dockerfile.pytorch.

torchvision was the one that mattered, because vLLM's timm reaches it whether or not anything here asks for it. It now has its own target — torchvision-wheel, built against this torch — so the serving image carries a working one. torchaudio and torchdata still have none and nothing imports them. See Serving stack.

docs.title: Make Targets
docs.text:
make help is authoritative and prints the live list with the values currently in effect. This page is a map of the groups; a target missing here is not a target that does not exist. Targets marked * in make help build and push to the registry, which needs the ci login.

make help          # every target, grouped
make list-vars     # every variable these targets read, with its value

docs.title: Registry (Zot)
docs.text:
Target zot-check Is the registry active and answering? zot-catalog List repositories zot-tags List tags for one repo — REPO=rocm-pytorch/base zot-wheels Published wheel artifacts, newest first — ZOT_TAGS=0 for all zot-wheelhouse The same with sizes, plus anything extracted into ./dist/wheels zot-logs Follow the registry's journal image-sizes Published image sizes, split into shared and own layers — LAYERS=1 for the breakdown image-data Aggregate those into dist/images/images.json for the docs site image-publish Commit that onto gh-pages; PUSH=1 to push zot-disk What the registry actually occupies, deduplicated — registry host only

Nothing here starts, stops or configures Zot — it is a bare-metal systemd service owned outside this repository. image-sizes and zot-disk answer different questions and disagree by a factor of two: see Image sizes.

docs.title: Compiler Cache
docs.text: Target cache-summary Endpoint, size, disk, deltas and per-target hit rates cache-check Can every build node reach the store? (fleet-check asks more) cache-logs Follow the WebDAV access log layer-summary Layer reuse per image on its most recent build

docs.title: Fleet
docs.text:
Target list-nodes Which manifest is in effect, and the nodes it declares fleet-apply Bring every node to the state the manifest claims (Ansible) fleet-check Read-only acceptance test: can each node do its job? builder-setup A buildx builder for every build node in the manifest builder-<node> One of them — builder-snoc-think, say builder-pool Every build node as one buildx builder (little used — see below) builder-status Every builder and its nodes builder-health Which builders can take work builder-load CPU, cores and load per node of $(BUILDER) builder-logs buildkitd's own log: registry auth, GC, connection failures builder-restart Restart buildkitd on $(BUILDER), clearing a wedged build

builder-ensure gates every build target on builder-health, so a build fails fast against a dead node rather than hanging. builder-restart drops only that node's in-memory build state.

builder-<node> is a pattern rule over the manifest's node names, so a new node needs no Makefile edit. The buildkitd config is baked in at create time — an existing builder does not pick up a later manifest change, and adopting one costs that node's content store: docker buildx rm snoc-think && make builder-snoc-think. See The fleet.

docs.title: Watching A Build
docs.text:
Target build-watch Live: history across every builder, a tail of each running build, layer reuse and cache deltas build-status Build records on $(BUILDER), with the node each ran on build-logs What a build's steps printed — BUILD=<id>, default most recent build-inspect Duration, step count, cached steps, VCS revision build-stop Cancel builds started from this repository 
make build-watch WATCH_BUILDERS=snoc-think WATCH_LINES=40 WATCH_INTERVAL=2

Two logs, easy to confuse

build-logs is the output of the build's steps — what a RUN printed. builder-logs is the daemon underneath, and it is where a registry failure, a DNS failure or a cache problem shows up, often while the build itself just looks slow.

build-stop works off a PID file (/tmp/.rocm-build.pids) that every bake invocation and the balancer write to. Matching command lines with pgrep -f killed the invoking shell, and the sibling project's builds.

docs.title: Build And Push
docs.text:
Every target has a build-<name> form and a push-<name> form. Four names do not match their bake target:

Make Bake target build-base / push-base pytorch-base build-runtime / push-runtime pytorch-run build-torch-wheel / push-torch-wheel pytorch-wheel build-triton-wheel / push-triton-wheel triton-wheel (noarch)

The rest are the obvious ones: pytorch, rocm-runtime, pytorch-src, aiter-wheel, torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel. Group targets are build-serving/push-serving, build-all/push-all (the default group) and push-wheels.

The build-only forms exist because the benchmark harness dispatches through make build-<name>, and a push- target writes to the registry, which the credential helper cannot do unattended.

fetch-<name>-wheel pulls a published wheel artifact into ./dist. build-cold builds COLD_TARGET (default pytorch) with neither layer cache nor compiler-cache hits.

build-all refuses BUILDER=snoc-pool

Scheduling makes every target its own bake invocation, so they cannot hand results to each other through target: contexts. Use push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool (scheduled, publishes) or build-all BUILDER=snoc-think (single builder, no push). See the balancer.

docs.title: Multiple Architectures
docs.text:
Target arches-<anything> Run any target once per architecture in ARCHES arches-list What ARCHES resolves to, with the tag each would produce wheel-index Fetch each architecture's wheels and build a PEP 503 index wheel-index-check Install each generated index into a throwaway venv wheels-publish Publish one architecture publicly — release + gh-pages (ARCH=) wheels-publish-dry Show what wheels-publish would do, touching nothing

arches-% takes any target name, not only the documented examples.

docs.title: Test And Serve
docs.text:
Target test The in-graph pytorch-test stage, which needs a GPU gpu-test Run a published image on a real GPU — GPU_HOST=, PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH= serve-vllm vLLM alone on GPU_HOST, no KV offload serve-stack vLLM plus the LMCache MP server serve-wait Block until /health answers serve-test Prove the KV cache is actually working (-baseline, -l2 variants) serve-logs Both containers, merged, live (-cache, -sorted variants) serve-status What is running on GPU_HOST serve-down Stop and remove

See Serving stack.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Target bench Run the harness — BENCH_SCENARIO=frozen\|cold\|warm\|hot\|all\|everything bench-report Render accumulated results as markdown bench-data Aggregate into dist/bench/bench.json for the docs site bench-publish Commit that onto gh-pages; PUSH=1 to push

See Performance.

docs.title: Performance Runs
docs.text:
Target perf-plan Which builder each wheel would land on; builds nothing perf-cold Cold parallel build of every wheel, fully instrumented perf-warm The same instrumentation on a warm build — caches on, pushes perf-report Render the newest run as markdown plus SVG charts perf-serve Serve the newest run's interactive chart on :8090 perf-serve-stop Stop it and free PERF_PORT perf-serve-status Whether one is running, and where perf-runs List collected runs, newest last perf-publish Commit a run onto gh-pages; PUSH=1 to push

The fleet flat out, rather than one target in isolation. Both build and push whatever the registry is missing first, so neither needs a manual bootstrap. PERF_ARCH, PERF_TARGETS and PERF_BIND configure them; see Instrumented fleet runs.

perf-serve and the published data/perf/ page are the same tool: perf-publish puts the chart perf-serve renders onto gh-pages, with a selector added across runs. Serve locally while a run is in flight — the page regenerates every 30 s and re-resolves which run is newest, so it picks up a run that started after the server did. Published runs are frozen and stop polling.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Target version-check Upstream releases vs published wheels vs our pins version-scrub Regenerate the version tables from rocm-bake.hcl version-scrub-check Fail if those generated tables are stale

version-check needs the network. version-scrub reads rocm-bake.hcl and nothing else, which is what lets version-scrub-check gate every pull request; the tables it generates live between <!-- BEGIN VERSIONS --> markers in README.md and in Bake variables.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Target docs-deps Create the docs venv from docs/requirements.txt docs-build Build into dist/site; fails on a broken internal link docs-serve Serve locally with live reload on :8000

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text: Target validate Is the bake file parseable? bake-plan Print the resolved build plan as JSON list-vars Every variable these targets read, with its value and source clean Remove built images locally, for every architecture in ARCHES clean-cache Drop locally-pulled cache images; Zot garbage-collects its own store setup zot-check then builder-setup

docs.title: Variables Worth Knowing
docs.text:
Variable Default FLEET snoc Which manifests/<name>.yml describes the fleet FLEET_MANIFEST — A manifest path directly, instead of FLEET BUILDER the manifest's default_builder Which builder, or the pool sentinel for the balancer ARCHES gfx950 gfx1201 gfx1250 What arches-* fans out over PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH gfx950 The architecture for one build TELEMETRY 1 0 skips the metrics wrapper BAKE_EXTRA — Arbitrary extra flags passed to bake GPU_HOST the manifest's gpu_node The machine with /dev/kfd; empty on a build-only fleet REPO rocm-pytorch/base What zot-tags lists ZOT_TAGS 5 Tags per repo in zot-wheels; 0 for all BENCH_SCENARIO all Which benchmark scenario make bench runs

Some variables only work from the environment

make <target> VAR=value works for anything the Makefile reads. But SCCACHE_LOG, PUBLISHED_INPUTS, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* overrides are read by bake, from the environment — so they need VAR=value make <target> instead.
